Higher scores help sustain regional employment, especially in lower-unemployment areas.

Local Labor Market Conditions

High unemployment (≥6.6%) worsens outcomes, particularly for low scorers from higher-income backgrounds.
Wages also matter: in lower-unemployment areas, students in counties with wages ≥83% of the state average are more likely to sustain regional employment.

Economic Status

Within high-unemployment contexts, low-income students (economic.status = 1) are more likely to sustain meaningful regional employment than their higher-income peers.


Overall Narrative
At 10 years after graduation, the pathway to sustaining meaningful regional employment depends most strongly on CTE engagement, moderated by SpecialEd needs, reading proficiency, and local economic conditions.

Students without CTE participation are at the highest risk of having no MN employment record.
SpecialEd students, even with CTE backgrounds, remain at higher risk of long-term disconnection.
Local unemployment and wages shape whether academically weaker students can stay employed regionally, with low-income students sometimes more anchored regionally than higher-income peers in tough labor markets.

In short, by Year 10, CTE engagement remains the primary anchor to regional employment, but SpecialEd needs and weak reading skills create enduring barriers, while labor market context and income level add important nuance to long-term outcomes.

title: Non-post-secondary graduates
text:
Overall summary
This analysis explored three contrasts in employment outcomes for non-college graduates:

Meaningful emp region vs. Meaningful emp MN
Meaningful emp region vs. Not meaningful, not attending ps
Meaningful emp region vs. No MN employment record, not attending ps

Across all outcomes, models show that regional employment is most strongly anchored by CTE engagement and undermined by SpecialEd needs, weak academics, and unfavorable economic contexts. Predictive strength declines from Year 1 to Year 10 as life paths diversify, but consistent patterns emerge.

Model Performance

Region vs. MN: Models perform slightly above baseline at Year 1 (78.3%) and then decline (66.8% at Year 5, 62.1% at Year 10).
Region vs. Not meaningful: Year 1 (65.7%), Year 5 (54.7%), and Year 10 (55.5%) all show limited but interpretable gains over baseline.
Region vs. No MN record: Year 1 (62.3%) shows strong improvement over baseline, with Year 5 (57.7%) and Year 10 (59.3%) holding modest gains.

Overall, Year 1 models provide the clearest separation, while later models mainly highlight persistent anchors and barriers.

Variable Importance Across Outcomes

CTE Engagement: The most consistent anchor across all contrasts and years. Both heavy course-taking and concentrator/completer status increase the likelihood of staying in meaningful regional employment.
SpecialEd Status: A strong and consistent predictor of disconnection — students with SpecialEd needs are much more likely to fall into “Not meaningful” or “No MN record.”
Academic Performance:

ACT scores matter most in Region vs. MN (mobility marker) and Region vs. Not meaningful (early anchor).
Reading (MCA.R) becomes increasingly relevant by Year 10, especially for differentiating Region vs. No MN record.

Economic Conditions: Local wages and unemployment rates shape outcomes at every stage, with higher wages anchoring students regionally and high unemployment increasing disconnection risk.
Socioeconomic Status (income): By Year 10, low-income students are sometimes more anchored regionally than higher-income peers, especially under weak labor markets.


Interpretation Across Years

Year 1 (Early Career Launch):

Regional employment hinges on local wages and academic preparation.
High ACT scorers often pursue statewide jobs, while CTE engagement keeps even high scorers in regional work.
SpecialEd students face steep barriers and are most likely to appear in “Not meaningful” or “No MN record.”

Year 5 (Mid-Career Sorting):

The landscape broadens to include SpecialEd status, CTE completion, academics, and economic context.
High academic performers increasingly pursue statewide employment.
CTE concentrators/completers remain regionally anchored, while SpecialEd students and low scorers are most at risk of disconnection.

Year 10 (Long-Run Outcomes):

Outcomes are shaped by CTE anchors vs. academic mobility markers.
ACT takers with high scores are the most mobile, while weak reading performance and SpecialEd needs predict long-term disconnection.
Labor markets (wages, unemployment) and income levels determine whether weaker students sustain regional jobs or exit Minnesota employment altogether.



Overall Narrative
Across all three comparisons, a clear pattern emerges:

Regional anchors: CTE engagement (especially completion), local wages, and in some cases low-income background.
Mobility markers: High ACT scores, ACT participation, and academic strength, which open pathways to statewide work.
Barriers to connection: SpecialEd needs, weak reading/math skills, and high local unemployment consistently predict disconnection from meaningful regional employment.

In short, regional employment is sustained when students engage deeply in CTE and are supported by favorable local labor markets, while academic high achievers are more mobile and SpecialEd students face enduring risks of disconnection.

Local wages and unemployment set the context, shaping whether weaker students remain employed regionally or fall out of the MN workforce.

Together, the findings emphasize that regional employment pathways are built on CTE engagement and supportive local economies, but require targeted supports for SpecialEd students and academically weaker groups to prevent long-term disconnection.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Attended Postsecondary Within First Year After High School Graduation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending postsecondary within the first year after high school and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 6425.35, Cramer’s V = 0.370, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 1218.28, Cramer’s V = 0.187, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 259.34, Cramer’s V = 0.114, p < .001, N = 19,828

The effect is very strong in the first year and weakens over time but remains statistically significant. The central pattern is that those who attend PS in the first year are much less likely to be in regional meaningful employment, while those who do not attend are far more likely to begin working in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students who did not attend PS within the first year had a much higher rate of regional meaningful employment (24.0%) compared to those who did attend (10.8%). Meanwhile, attenders were overwhelmingly in postsecondary (71.8% vs. 18.2%). This highlights the immediate split: PS attenders pursue education, while non‑attenders move directly into local work.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment remains higher among non‑attenders (32.7% vs. 23.2%). However, PS attenders surpass non‑attenders in statewide meaningful employment (18.2% vs. 11.4%). Disconnection is higher for non‑attenders (25.7% vs. 18.0%), reflecting weaker long‑term stability.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment continues to favor non‑attenders (34.4% vs. 26.6%). PS attenders retain an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 14.0%), while disconnection is far higher for non‑attenders (36.1% vs. 28.0%). This long‑term pattern confirms that early PS attendance pulls students away from regional work but enhances their broader statewide outcomes, while non‑attenders embed more deeply in the regional workforce.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Ever Attended Postsecondary (attended.ps)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between ever attending postsecondary and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 21,822.13, Cramer’s V = 0.683, p < .001, N = 46,777【724†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 4,066.08, Cramer’s V = 0.342, p < .001, N = 34,683【725†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 372.88, Cramer’s V = 0.137, p < .001, N = 19,828【726†source】

The effect is extremely strong in the first year but declines steadily over time. The central pattern is that students who attended postsecondary are far less likely to be in regional meaningful employment early on, though they become more evenly distributed between regional and statewide employment later.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students who did not attend PS show much higher regional meaningful employment (19.9% vs. 13.3%). However, their outcomes also include far more disconnection: 44.2% “not meaningful” and 30.1% “no MN record” compared to 10.5% and 3.5% among attenders. By contrast, attenders are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (69.1%). This reflects a sharp early divide: non‑attenders attach to local jobs or disconnect, while attenders delay employment for education【724†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment becomes slightly higher for attenders (27.5% vs. 23.9%), and statewide meaningful employment is also stronger among attenders (16.5% vs. 11.7%). Meanwhile, disconnection is far more common among non‑attenders (27.4% “not meaningful” and 37.0% “no record”) compared to 19% and 15% for attenders. Thus, by five years, attenders gain more stable and broader employment outcomes, while non‑attenders remain more vulnerable【725†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment favors attenders (31.4% vs. 23.0%), and their advantage in statewide meaningful employment (21.1% vs. 14.4%) continues. Non‑attenders remain much more disconnected (41.7% “no record” vs. 29.2% among attenders). Long‑term, this confirms that attending postsecondary—even if not immediately—enhances both regional and statewide employment outcomes, while non‑attenders remain more likely to disconnect【726†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that postsecondary attendance strongly reduces early local workforce entry but leads to more stable and broader employment later, whereas non‑attenders enter regional work early but remain at higher risk of disconnection.

Thus by five years, attenders are more successful statewide, while non‑attenders show weaker stability and higher disconnection【713†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment continues to be higher for attenders (31.6%) compared to non‑attenders (23.0%). Attenders also remain stronger in statewide meaningful employment (21.6% vs. 14.4%). By contrast, non‑attenders face higher disconnection (41.7% “no MN record” vs. 28.9% for attenders). title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation (ps.grad)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 15,285.21, Cramer’s V = 0.600, p < .001, N = 42,459【736†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 4,882.22, Cramer’s V = 0.378, p < .001, N = 34,144【737†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 476.15, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 19,828【738†source】

The effect is very strong in the first year, moderate by year 5, and still significant though weaker at year 10. The pattern shows that graduates are initially concentrated in continued postsecondary enrollment, but over time they transition into statewide meaningful employment and maintain somewhat stronger outcomes than non‑graduates.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Postsecondary graduates are overwhelmingly recorded as still attending PS (77.4%), compared to only 19.4% of non‑graduates. Regional meaningful employment is lower for graduates (11.6% vs. 19.2%), while non‑graduates are far more likely to fall into not meaningful (35%) or no MN record (20.8%). This shows the early divide: graduates are embedded in education, while non‑graduates more often enter local work or disconnection【736†source】.
Year 5: By this point, regional meaningful employment is similar between the two groups (26.9% graduates vs. 26.3% non‑graduates). However, graduates are more likely to achieve statewide meaningful employment (18.0% vs. 12.6%) and remain more represented in ongoing postsecondary enrollment (27.4% vs. 4.2%). Non‑graduates are much more disconnected, with 27.3% in “not meaningful” and 29.6% with no MN record【737†source】.
Year 10: Regional meaningful employment slightly favors graduates (33.0% vs. 25.6%). Graduates also maintain a strong advantage in statewide meaningful employment (23.4% vs. 15.6%). By contrast, non‑graduates are far more disconnected (36.7% “no MN record” vs. 28.0% for graduates). Long‑term, this confirms that postsecondary graduation enhances both regional and statewide employment outcomes, while non‑graduates are more likely to face disconnection【738†source】.
Overall, postsecondary graduation is a critical predictor of long‑term stability, reducing disconnection and improving both regional and statewide employment, while non‑graduates remain more vulnerable.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
ACT Composite Score
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between ACT Composite Score and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 27079) = 387.39, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 20617) = 159.11, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 10486) = 119.50, p < .001

The results show a clear and consistent pattern: students with higher ACT scores are more likely to attend postsecondary and later secure meaningful statewide employment, while students with lower ACT scores are more concentrated in regional meaningful jobs, not meaningful employment, or disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees have ACT scores ~2.8 points higher than those in regional meaningful employment (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.88) and No MN record (+1.43) also score above regional meaningful (both p < .001).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is tied to lower ACT scores, while higher scores track into education and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+1.87), statewide meaningful (+1.84), and No MN record (+1.69) all score significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful is ~0.62 higher than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment continues to come from lower ACT backgrounds, while higher scores predict broader education and statewide employment.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+1.64) and No MN record (+1.75) have higher ACT scores than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.43) is also above regional meaningful (p = .005).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment is consistently tied to lower ACT scores, while higher scores are associated with statewide employment or exit from tracked MN employment.
Overall, the ACT Composite Score reinforces a strong sorting effect: higher scores steer students toward education and statewide jobs, while regional meaningful employment is more common among lower scorers.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Total CTE Courses Taken
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the number of CTE courses taken and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 45696) = 232.40, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 33828) = 104.15, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19320) = 36.17, p < .001

The results show a consistent pattern: students who took more CTE courses are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment, while students with fewer CTE courses lean toward postsecondary, statewide, or disconnected pathways.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Regional meaningful employment is associated with higher CTE course counts compared to postsecondary (−0.72, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.21, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.37, p < .001).
- Postsecondary students have the lowest CTE course counts, confirming that heavier CTE load ties directly into early regional work.
Year 5:
- Regional meaningful again shows higher CTE courses than postsecondary (−0.61, p < .001), meaningful MN (−0.44, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.33, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.45, p < .001).
- Postsecondary and statewide workers come from lower CTE course backgrounds.
- Takeaway: at five years, regional meaningful work is strongly linked to CTE engagement, while those with fewer CTE courses are dispersed across statewide or disconnected outcomes.
Year 10:
- Regional meaningful still has higher CTE courses compared to statewide meaningful (−0.31, p < .001) and no MN record (−0.31, p < .001).
- Not meaningful outcomes also show slightly higher CTE courses than regional (+0.21, p < .001), reflecting a mixed subgroup.
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment is still concentrated among heavier CTE participants, reinforcing CTE as a strong predictor of regional attachment.
Overall, total CTE course load demonstrates that increased CTE participation anchors students more firmly in regional employment, while lighter CTE engagement is linked to education and broader employment pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
ACT Test Participation (Took ACT)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the ACT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 6187.26, Cramer’s V = 0.364, p < .001, N = 46,777【554†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 1583.75, Cramer’s V = 0.214, p < .001, N = 34,683【555†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 397.81, Cramer’s V = 0.142, p < .001, N = 19,828【556†source】

The strength of association is very strong in the first year and declines over time, but remains statistically significant. The key pattern is that ACT takers are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Non‑ACT students show much higher regional meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 12.1%) and are more likely to appear in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes (≈20% each). ACT participants overwhelmingly attend postsecondary (62.6% vs. 27.2%), illustrating a sharp divide between direct work and education pathways【554†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is still higher among non‑ACT students (28.7% vs. 25.0%), but ACT takers gain ground in statewide meaningful employment (17.8% vs. 11.3%). Postsecondary attendance is notably higher among ACT students (21.1% vs. 8.6%). Disconnection remains higher for non‑ACT (26.6% vs. 17.2%)【555†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment narrows (29.9% non‑ACT vs. 28.6% ACT). ACT takers surpass non‑takers in statewide meaningful employment (24.2% vs. 13.9%), while non‑ACT students remain more tied to regional employment. Disconnection is still higher for non‑ACT students (33.7% vs. 31.3%). The long‑term trajectory suggests that ACT takers shift into broader statewide employment, while non‑takers retain a stronger regional employment profile【556†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Math (MCA.M)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Math scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42550) = 1344.53, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 33107) = 152.39, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 18728) = 94.98, p < .001

The results show an especially strong relationship in the first year, with effects tapering but still significant through Year 10. The key pattern is that higher MCA Math scores are linked to postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment and weaker outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score much higher than regional meaningful (+0.58, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful is also above regional meaningful (+0.07, p = .026).
- Not meaningful (−0.06) and No MN record (−0.17) score lower than regional meaningful (p ≤ .001).
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful employment is positioned between low‑scoring disconnected outcomes and high‑scoring education pathways.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.28) and statewide meaningful (+0.27) both score significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.08) and No MN record (−0.24) score below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful work is associated with lower scores relative to statewide and postsecondary, but still stronger than disconnected categories.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.29) remains higher than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record shows a mixed pattern: one contrast indicates higher scores (+0.13, p < .001) while another shows lower scores (−0.15, p < .001), reflecting sub‑patterns in this group.
- Not meaningful (−0.10 to −0.38) scores consistently lower than regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful jobs remain linked to mid‑range math scores, lower than statewide/postsecondary but higher than disconnected outcomes.
Overall, MCA Math reinforces the trend seen in other MCA measures: higher achievement channels students into education and statewide employment, while regional meaningful employment is associated with lower but not the lowest scores, positioning it as a middle pathway.

title: Final Wrap-Up: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota

This final synthesis combines findings across all four sections: Demographics, High School Characteristics, High School Accomplishments, and Postsecondary Experiences.

SpecialEd Status and Race/Ethnicity stand out as the strongest demographic predictors, particularly in shaping early outcomes.

Gender, Economic Status, and English Learner status show weaker associations that fade quickly.

Overall, demographics set context but are less determinative compared to later factors.





Local context (rural/urban, unemployment, wage levels) influences early pathways, especially pushing some students into immediate work.

These effects diminish with time, suggesting that structural local factors matter most at the point of high school exit, but individual choices and credentials overtake them later.





Clear split between academic and technical tracks:

College-prep measures (ACT, PSEO, MCA, AP, SAT) → lead to postsecondary and statewide employment, reducing regional attachment.

CTE measures (CTE achievement, total courses) → tie directly to regional meaningful employment, with effects persisting 10 years out.


MCA Math in particular emerges as the strongest achievement predictor across all accomplishment variables.





This is the most powerful section overall. Postsecondary attendance and completion dominate long-term outcomes.

Attenders and graduates show stronger statewide and stable employment, while non-attenders and non-graduates enter regional jobs early but face greater disconnection risk long-term.

Institution type, credential level, and location add nuance:

Regional and 2-year pathways → strengthen regional attachment.

4-year and out-of-state pathways → expand statewide opportunities but reduce regional ties.







Across all sections, a consistent theme emerges:
- Regional meaningful employment is most strongly predicted by career/technical education in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.
- Statewide meaningful employment and mobility are driven by academic achievement, 4-year college pathways, and higher credentials.
- Disconnection is most common among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker academic/CTE preparation, compounded by local economic stressors.
In sum, the evidence highlights two diverging but equally important pathways:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → stronger anchoring in the regional workforce.
Both play vital roles in shaping the Northeast Minnesota labor market and should be considered complementary in policy and planning.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Wages as Percent of State (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between relative county wages and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on wage percent across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46751) = 15.33, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 24.64, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19824) = 11.82, p < .001

Although effect sizes are small, the relationships are consistent. The primary finding is that graduates from counties with higher relative wages are more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while those from lower‑wage counties are more likely to be in meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees come from higher‑wage counties than nearly all other groups (Δ ≈ +0.009 vs. regional meaningful, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also slightly higher than regional meaningful (Δ ≈ +0.006–0.008, p ≤ .05).
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful employment is linked to lower‑wage counties, while education is linked to higher‑wage contexts.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary attendees again come from higher‑wage counties (+0.009 vs. meaningful MN, p < .001).
- Regional meaningful employment is associated with lower‑wage contexts compared to statewide meaningful (Δ = −0.009, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are slightly higher than regional meaningful (Δ ≈ +0.005–0.006, both p < .01).
- Takeaway: statewide meaningful employment and further schooling are linked to higher‑wage counties, while regional meaningful work remains concentrated in lower‑wage areas.
Year 10:
- Regional meaningful employment continues to be tied to lower‑wage counties than statewide meaningful (Δ = −0.007, p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.004, p = .008) and No MN record (+0.006, p < .001) are also above regional meaningful.
- Takeaway: a decade out, the pattern solidifies — regional meaningful employment is most strongly associated with lower‑wage counties, while higher‑wage counties are more tied to education, statewide meaningful, or disconnected pathways.
Overall, the wage context shows a consistent divide: regional meaningful jobs are concentrated in lower‑wage counties, whereas higher‑wage counties foster postsecondary and statewide pathways.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
High School Rural–Urban Context (Dem_Desc)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between rural–urban context and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 54.72, Cramer’s V = 0.024, p < .001, N = 46,777【474†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 201.14, Cramer’s V = 0.054, p < .001, N = 34,683【476†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 75.40, Cramer’s V = 0.044, p < .001, N = 19,828【477†source】

The associations are weak but consistent. The primary pattern is that students from Urban/town/rural mix areas are most likely to achieve meaningful employment in the region, while those from Entirely rural areas are least likely to do so, especially by Years 5 and 10.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for Urban/town/rural mix (15.8%), followed by Town/rural mix (14.9%), and lowest for Entirely rural (11.8%). Postsecondary attendance is nearly identical across groups (~48%). Disconnection is slightly higher for Entirely rural (12.1%) compared to others (≈11.6–11.9%)【474†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Urban/town/rural mix leads in regional meaningful employment (27.8%), compared to Town/rural mix (24.3%) and Entirely rural (20.2%). Interestingly, Entirely rural graduates show higher statewide meaningful employment (23.5%), indicating more attachment to jobs outside their immediate region. Disconnection is modestly lower for Entirely rural (19.7%) compared to others (≈20.8–21.9%)【476†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The pattern persists. Urban/town/rural mix maintains the highest regional meaningful employment (30.3%), while Entirely rural remains lowest (22.8%). Entirely rural students, however, hold the highest statewide meaningful employment share (26.9%), reinforcing the pattern of outward mobility for work. Disconnection is high across all groups (~30–33%) but does not vary sharply by rural–urban context【477†source】.
Overall, the rural–urban context shows weak but clear differences: students from more urban-influenced areas are more likely to remain in meaningful employment within the region, while those from entirely rural schools are more likely to find meaningful employment elsewhere in Minnesota.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
English Learner Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between English Learner (EL) status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 1649.35, Cramer’s V = 0.188, p < .001, N = 46,777【448†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 459.23, Cramer’s V = 0.115, p < .001, N = 34,683【449†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 124.44, Cramer’s V = 0.079, p < .001, N = 19,828【450†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, though the relationship remains significant. The primary relationship is that English Learner students are much less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be disconnected or in not meaningful employment, while non-EL students are more likely to pursue postsecondary and secure meaningful regional employment over time.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Non-EL students are more likely to be attending postsecondary (49.2% vs. 16.6%) and in meaningful regional employment (15.5% vs. 11.8%). EL students are disproportionately represented in not meaningful (31.8% vs. 20.4%) and disconnected outcomes (35.8% vs. 10.6%). This shows a sharp early divide.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment grows for both groups, but the gap persists (26.7% non-EL vs. 21.1% EL). EL students continue to be much less likely to be in postsecondary (3.7% vs. 16.6%) and more likely to be disconnected (38.1% vs. 20.3%). By this point, EL students are more than 15 percentage points less likely to secure regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: Non-EL students further strengthen their advantage in meaningful regional employment (29.6% vs. 17.4%) and statewide meaningful employment (19.7% vs. 7.6%). Nearly half of EL students (48.3%) remain disconnected, compared to 32.0% of non-EL students. The long-term trajectory shows that English Learners face enduring disadvantages in both education and attachment to meaningful regional employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Race/Ethnicity
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between race/ethnicity and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(16) = 737.61, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 41,205【435†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(16) = 363.79, Cramer’s V = 0.051, p < .001, N = 34,683【437†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 198.54, Cramer’s V = 0.058, p < .001, N = 19,828【438†source】

The associations are weak but consistent across time, suggesting that while race/ethnicity matters, the effect sizes are smaller compared to other demographic variables. The primary relationship is that White students are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment and attend postsecondary, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students are more often in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: White students show higher rates of postsecondary attendance (50.1%) and meaningful regional employment (15.3%) compared to most other groups. American Indian students are less likely to attend postsecondary (32.2%) and more likely to be in not meaningful employment (28.8%) or disconnected (18.7%). Black and Hispanic students also face higher shares of not meaningful or disconnected outcomes, while Asian/PI students lean toward postsecondary enrollment (48.1%) but have low regional employment (8.3%).
5 Years After Graduation: White students continue to dominate in meaningful regional employment (27.1%) and statewide meaningful work (15.6%). American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students remain underrepresented in regional employment (15.9–19.8%) and have higher shares in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. Asian/PI students, though still lower in regional employment (15.9%), maintain stronger postsecondary presence (18.9%). The disparities remain persistent.
10 Years After Graduation: White students further strengthen their advantage in meaningful regional employment (30.1%) and statewide meaningful work (19.9%). American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students remain behind, with regional employment in the 13–21% range and higher disconnection rates (44–50% for Black and Hispanic). Asian/PI students continue to have weaker attachment to regional employment (15.6%), though they retain moderate statewide meaningful employment. The long-term pattern highlights systemic disparities in both education and labor market outcomes, with White students benefiting most from regional meaningful employment opportunities.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Key Findings

Demographics are the strongest and most consistent predictors across all three outcomes.

Economic Status: Economically disadvantaged students lagged behind at every stage—less likely to enroll immediately, less likely to attend at all, and much less likely to graduate.
Race/Ethnicity: White and Asian/PI students consistently had higher enrollment and graduation rates, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students faced persistent barriers at all stages, with the largest disparities at completion.
Special Education Status: Students with special education status showed markedly lower rates of enrollment, attendance, and especially graduation.

High School Characteristics showed weak associations.

School Locale: Rural, mixed, and urban settings had minimal differences in postsecondary pathways.
Community Economic Conditions: Students from lower-unemployment, higher-wage areas were modestly more likely to enroll, attend, and graduate, but these effects were smaller than individual-level demographics or accomplishments.

High School Accomplishments were powerful predictors, especially for enrollment and graduation.

Academic Achievement: ACT and MCA scores (particularly Reading and Science) were strongly linked to both immediate enrollment and graduation, showing that academic readiness is a key driver of persistence and attainment.
PSEO Participation: The single strongest programmatic predictor across all outcomes. PSEO students were much more likely to enroll immediately, attend at all, and eventually graduate.
CTE Involvement: Higher CTE course-taking and concentrator/completor status were associated with lower likelihood of both enrollment and graduation, suggesting that intensive CTE pathways align more with direct workforce entry than with postsecondary progression.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Overall Conclusion:
Tier 1 analysis reveals that postsecondary access and attainment are shaped by both structural inequities and academic preparation. Demographic barriers—economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity—consistently depress outcomes at every stage. Academic readiness (ACT and MCA scores) and program participation (especially PSEO) are the most powerful positive predictors of successful transitions and completion. In contrast, CTE intensity is inversely associated with postsecondary outcomes, reflecting its alignment with alternative workforce pathways.
Together, these findings suggest that strategies to improve postsecondary success must focus on closing equity gaps, bolstering academic readiness, and expanding access to PSEO and similar dual-enrollment programs, while also balancing the role of CTE in supporting both workforce entry and potential academic progression.

attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad

Summary
Key Findings by Variable Group
Demographics

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.246. Non-disadvantaged students had much higher immediate enrollment (72.1%) than disadvantaged students (47.6%). Economic disadvantage is a major barrier to direct enrollment.

Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.096. White (67%) and Asian/PI (58.7%) students enrolled at higher rates, while American Indian (45.8%), Black (51.4%), and Hispanic (51.6%) students enrolled at lower rates.

Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.278. Students without special education status were far more likely to enroll immediately (68.6%) than those with special education status (32.6%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.022. Very weak differences across rural, mixed, and urban contexts (all ~62%).

Average Unemployment Rate: F(2, 49813) = 302.20, p < .001. Students from higher-unemployment areas were less likely to enroll immediately.

Average Wages (as % of State Average): F(2, 49813) = 33.08, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were slightly more likely to attend postsecondary (immediately or later).

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(2, 28493) = 396.75, p < .001. Higher ACT scores strongly predicted immediate enrollment, with immediate enrollees scoring about 2 points higher than non-attendees.

PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.295. PSEO participants enrolled immediately at very high rates (76.8%) compared to non-participants (48.2%).

CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.052. CTE concentrators/completors were less likely to enroll immediately (57.9%) than participants (64.9%) or non-CTE students (65.7%).

Total CTE Courses Taken: F(2, 49813) = 301.90, p < .001. More CTE courses were associated with lower immediate enrollment.

MCA Math: F(2, 47621) = 885.58, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored much higher (0.50 points above delayed enrollees).

MCA Reading: F(2, 47319) = 1475.87, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored substantially higher (0.46 points above non-attendees).

MCA Science: F(2, 40378) = 1025.37, p < .001. Immediate enrollees scored much higher (0.41 points above non-attendees); no difference between delayed and non-attendees.




Relative Importance of Predictors (Ranked by Effect Size/Strength of Association):

Special Education Status (Cramer’s V = 0.278) – strong demographic predictor.
PSEO Participation (Cramer’s V = 0.295) – strongest programmatic predictor.
Economic Status (Cramer’s V = 0.246) – major structural barrier.
MCA Reading (F = 1475.87) – strongest academic achievement predictor.
MCA Science (F = 1025.37) – strong academic predictor.
MCA Math (F = 885.58) – strong academic predictor.
ACT Composite Score (F = 396.75) – important test-based predictor.
Average Unemployment Rate (F = 302.20) – moderate community context effect.
Total CTE Courses Taken (F = 301.90) – more courses linked to weaker transition.
Race/Ethnicity (Cramer’s V = 0.096) – modest but meaningful disparities.
Average Wages (F = 33.08) – small community effect.
CTE Achievement (Cramer’s V = 0.052) – weak association.
School Locale (Cramer’s V = 0.022) – negligible differences.


Conclusion:
Immediate postsecondary enrollment is shaped most strongly by student characteristics (economic status, special education status, race/ethnicity), program participation (PSEO), and academic achievement (MCA and ACT scores). Community economic conditions (unemployment and wages) also matter but to a lesser extent, while school locale and CTE achievement have minimal influence. This suggests that interventions targeting equity gaps, strengthening academic preparation, and expanding access to PSEO could have the greatest impact on improving direct transitions to postsecondary education.


Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.246, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students enrolled immediately at much higher rates (72.1%) than economically disadvantaged students (47.6%). Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to never attend (46.1% vs. 24.0%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.096, p < .001. White (67%) and Asian/PI (58.7%) students had the highest immediate enrollment. American Indian students had the lowest (45.8%), while Black (51.4%) and Hispanic (51.6%) students also enrolled at below-average rates.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.278, p < .001. Students without special education status were much more likely to enroll immediately (68.6%) than those with special education status (32.6%). Special education students were more likely to never attend (62.2% vs. 26.7%).

Conclusion:
Demographic factors play a significant role in shaping immediate postsecondary enrollment. Economic disadvantage and special education status are linked to substantially lower rates of transition, with both groups far more likely to never enroll. Race and ethnicity also matter, with White and Asian/PI students showing stronger transitions and American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students facing greater barriers. Overall, these patterns highlight persistent equity gaps in postsecondary access immediately after high school.

Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to never attend postsecondary (“Did not attend ps”: 46.1% vs. 24.0%) and somewhat more likely to delay enrollment beyond the first year (“No”: 6.3% vs. 3.9%).
Conclusion:
Economic disadvantage is moderately and significantly associated with lower immediate postsecondary enrollment and higher non-enrollment. Students not economically disadvantaged transition directly to college at much higher rates, while economically disadvantaged students are more likely to delay or never attend.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Attended.ps

Summary
Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: φ = 0.228, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to attend (76%) than disadvantaged students (53.9%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001. White (72.4%) and Asian/PI (65.7%) students had the highest attendance, while American Indian students (51.8%) had the lowest, with Black (57.7%) and Hispanic (58.7%) also below average.
Special Education Status: φ = 0.273, p < .001. Attendance was much higher for students without special education status (73.3%) compared to those with it (37.8%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.029, p < .001. Differences across rural, town/rural mix, and urban/town/rural mix were minimal (65–69%).
Average Unemployment Rate: F(1, 49814) = 428.40, p < .001. Students from lower-unemployment areas were more likely to attend.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(1, 49814) = 65.84, p < .001. Attendees came from areas with slightly higher average wages.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(1, 28494) = 739.92, p < .001. Attendees scored about 2 points higher than non-attendees.
PSEO Participation: φ = 0.279, p < .001. Participation strongly boosted attendance (79.8% vs. 53.3%).
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001. Concentrators/completors had lower attendance (62.9%) than participants (69.6%) and students with no CTE (70.4%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(1, 49814) = 565.70, p < .001. Non-attendees had taken more CTE courses.
MCA Math: F(1, 47622) = 1220.58, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.35 points higher.
MCA Reading: F(1, 47320) = 2654.13, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.44 points higher, the strongest MCA predictor.
MCA Science: F(1, 40379) = 1721.96, p < .001. Attendees scored 0.39 points higher.


Overall Conclusion:
Postsecondary attendance is most strongly influenced by demographic barriers (economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity), program participation (PSEO), and academic achievement (ACT and MCA scores, especially Reading). Community economic conditions (unemployment and wages) also play a role, though weaker, while CTE involvement shows an inverse relationship—students taking more CTE courses or reaching concentrator/completor status were less likely to attend.
Taken together, the results suggest that promoting equitable access to rigorous academics, reducing economic and special education barriers, and expanding opportunities like PSEO may be the most effective levers for improving overall postsecondary participation.



Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: φ = 0.228, p < .001. Postsecondary attendance was higher for non-disadvantaged students (76%) than for economically disadvantaged students (53.9%). Disadvantaged students were almost twice as likely to never attend (46.1% vs. 24%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001. Attendance was highest for White (72.4%) and Asian/PI (65.7%) students. Attendance was lower among Hispanic (58.7%) and Black (57.7%) students, and lowest among American Indian students (51.8%). Students classified as “Unknown” also showed below-average rates (55.8%).
Special Education Status: φ = 0.273, p < .001. Students without special education status were far more likely to attend postsecondary (73.3%) compared to students with special education status (37.8%). Special education students were more than twice as likely to never attend (62.2% vs. 26.7%).

Conclusion:
Demographic factors are strongly associated with whether students ever attend postsecondary. Economic disadvantage and special education status present the largest barriers, while racial disparities are also significant, with American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students less likely to attend. These findings highlight that systemic inequities in access persist even when considering postsecondary attendance at any point after high school.

ps.grad

Summary
Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: φ = 0.270, p < .001. Graduation was much higher among non-disadvantaged students (53.1%) compared to economically disadvantaged students (25.7%). Disadvantaged students were nearly three times as likely not to graduate.
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.169, p < .001 (Unknown removed). White (49.2%) and Asian/PI (44.7%) students had the highest graduation rates, while Hispanic (31.3%), Black (21.6%), and American Indian (20.8%) students had much lower rates.
Special Education Status: φ = 0.262, p < .001. Students without special education status graduated at far higher rates (48.2%) than those with it (13.2%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.022, p < .001. Graduation rates were very similar across rural (39.2%), town/rural mix (41.6%), and urban/town/rural mix (43.2%).
Average Unemployment Rate: F(1, 44033) = 572.00, p < .001. Graduates came from areas with unemployment rates about 0.33 percentage points lower than non-graduates.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(1, 44033) = 43.37, p < .001. Graduates came from areas with wages about 0.33 percentage points higher than non-graduates.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(1, 24476) = 1619.08, p < .001. Graduates scored about 2.41 points higher than non-graduates.
PSEO Participation: φ = 0.308, p < .001. Graduation was much more common among PSEO participants (57%) than non-participants (26.7%).
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.103, p < .001. Concentrators/completors had the lowest graduation rates (35.5%), while participants (42.7%) and non-CTE students (47.5%) graduated at higher rates.
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(1, 44033) = 693.05, p < .001. Non-graduates had taken about 0.60 more CTE courses than graduates.
MCA Math: F(1, 41955) = 1748.50, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.41 points higher than non-graduates.
MCA Reading: F(1, 41687) = 3087.39, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.47 points higher, the strongest MCA predictor.
MCA Science: F(1, 34774) = 2188.12, p < .001. Graduates scored 0.44 points higher.


Overall Conclusion:
Postsecondary graduation is shaped most strongly by student-level factors. Economic disadvantage and special education status are powerful barriers, while race and ethnicity reveal deep inequities in attainment. Among school-related experiences, PSEO participation stands out as the most influential positive predictor of graduation. Academic preparation (ACT and MCA scores, especially Reading and Science) also plays a major role. In contrast, greater CTE involvement—both in number of courses and concentrator/completor status—is linked to lower graduation rates, suggesting that heavy CTE pathways align more with workforce entry than degree attainment. Community economic conditions (lower unemployment and higher wages) show modest but consistent associations.
Taken together, these findings highlight that supporting equity, strengthening academic readiness, and expanding dual-enrollment opportunities like PSEO are critical levers for increasing postsecondary completion rates.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
highest.cred.level

Key Findings Across Variable Groups
Demographics

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.264, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to earn a bachelor’s or higher (46.2% vs. 20.4%), while disadvantaged students disproportionately stopped at “Some college” (49.2% vs. 26.6%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.088, p < .001. White (40.9%) and Asian/PI (52.5%) students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment. Black (20.1%), Hispanic (26.7%), and American Indian (19.5%) students were far more likely to leave with “Some college” or sub-associate credentials.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.233, p < .001. Students with special education status were overwhelmingly concentrated in “Some college” (61.6%), with very few earning a bachelor’s+ (6.9%) compared to non-special education students (41.4%).

High School Characteristics

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.028, p < .001. Credential attainment was nearly identical across rural, mixed, and urban/town/rural schools.
Average Unemployment Rate: F(3, 28012) = 9.11, p < .001. Students from higher-unemployment areas were slightly more likely to stop at sub-associate levels, while those from lower-unemployment areas were somewhat more likely to reach bachelor’s+.
Average Wages (% of State Average): F(3, 28012) = 6.70, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were modestly more likely to earn bachelor’s+, while those from lower-wage areas were slightly more likely to stop short.

High School Accomplishments

ACT Composite Score: F(3, 19493) = 1165.82, p < .001. Higher ACT scores strongly predicted bachelor’s+ attainment. “Some college” students scored similarly to associate earners, indicating persistence rather than readiness drove non-completion.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.308, p < .001. PSEO participants were more than twice as likely to earn a bachelor’s+ (50.5% vs. 22.2%) and much less likely to stop at “Some college.”
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.140, p < .001. CTE concentrators/completors were more likely to stop at associate degrees (28.2%) or “Some college” (38.9%) and less likely to reach bachelor’s+ (25.6%). Non-CTE students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment (47%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(3, 28012) = 471.36, p < .001. More CTE courses were associated with lower attainment; bachelor’s+ earners took the fewest CTE courses, while sub-associate and “Some college” groups took the most.
MCA Math, Reading, Science: All strongly associated with credential level (F > 850, p < .001). Bachelor’s+ earners consistently scored 0.3–0.6 points higher across subjects, with Reading and Science showing the strongest predictive value.




Overall Conclusion
The level of postsecondary credential earned is shaped most powerfully by demographic factors and academic accomplishments. Economic disadvantage, special education status, and race/ethnicity all create steep barriers, concentrating students in sub-associate outcomes or “Some college” without completion. In contrast, strong academic preparation (ACT, MCA scores) and PSEO participation sharply increase the likelihood of earning a bachelor’s or higher degree. Intensive CTE engagement, while supporting workforce readiness, is consistently associated with lower attainment levels, especially associate degrees or non-completion.
Community context (unemployment and wages) exerts a modest effect, but school locale has virtually no impact. Overall, Tier 2 results highlight that rigorous academics, equitable supports, and access to dual-enrollment opportunities are critical levers for ensuring students not only graduate but also achieve higher levels of credential attainment.



Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.264, p < .001. Non-disadvantaged students were far more likely to complete a bachelor’s or higher degree (46.2% vs. 20.4%) while disadvantaged students disproportionately left with “Some college” and no degree (49.2% vs. 26.6%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.088, p < .001. White (40.9%) and Asian/PI (52.5%) students were most likely to earn bachelor’s or higher degrees, while American Indian (19.5%), Black (20.1%), and Hispanic (26.7%) students disproportionately stopped short, often leaving with no degree.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.233, p < .001. Students with special education status were overwhelmingly concentrated in “Some college” (61.6%), with only 6.9% earning a bachelor’s or higher, compared to 41.4% of non-special education students.

Conclusion:
Demographic factors play a major role in shaping the highest credential attained. Economic disadvantage and special education status are the strongest barriers, sharply reducing the likelihood of earning a bachelor’s or higher degree. Racial disparities also persist, with White and Asian/PI students attaining higher levels of education, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students are much more likely to leave postsecondary without completing a credential. These patterns highlight that inequities extend well beyond access and graduation, influencing the ultimate level of educational attainment students are able to achieve.

ACT Composite Score: F(3, 19493) = 1165.82, p < .001. Students earning a bachelor’s or higher scored 3–4 points above those stopping at associate or sub-associate levels. “Some college” students had ACT scores similar to associate earners, suggesting non-completion is tied more to persistence than readiness.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.308, p < .001. PSEO participants were more than twice as likely to earn a bachelor’s or higher (50.5% vs. 22.2%) and far less likely to leave with “Some college” (23.9% vs. 44.9%). Associate and sub-associate outcomes were nearly identical between groups.
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.140, p < .001. Concentrators/completors were less likely to earn bachelor’s+ (25.6%) and more likely to stop at associate (28.2%) or “Some college” (38.9%). Non-CTE students had the highest bachelor’s+ attainment (47%).
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(3, 28012) = 471.36, p < .001. Students who earned bachelor’s+ took fewer CTE courses, while those with sub-associate or “Some college” outcomes had taken more. Largest gap: bachelor’s+ vs. sub-associate, with >1.3 course difference.
MCA Math: F(3, 27568) = 925.88, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.45–0.66 points higher than other groups. Lower scores characterized sub-associate and “Some college” outcomes.
MCA Reading: F(3, 27410) = 1053.96, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.32–0.59 points higher than other groups, making reading one of the strongest predictors of higher attainment.
MCA Science: F(3, 22192) = 854.01, p < .001. Bachelor’s+ earners scored 0.41–0.60 points higher than other groups, while “Some college” and sub-associate students scored notably lower.

Conclusion:
High school accomplishments are among the most powerful predictors of the highest credential earned. PSEO participation stands out as the strongest programmatic factor, dramatically increasing the likelihood of bachelor’s or higher attainment. Academic performance (ACT, MCA Reading, and MCA Science especially) is tightly linked to ultimate attainment, differentiating bachelor’s+ earners from those who stop earlier. In contrast, greater CTE engagement (more courses and concentrator/completor status) is associated with lower levels of attainment, with students more likely to finish at the associate level or leave with “Some college.” Overall, rigorous academics and early postsecondary experiences strongly support higher credential attainment, while intensive CTE pathways align more with sub-baccalaureate outcomes.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
ps.grad.location
Tier 3 examined how demographic factors, high school characteristics, and high school accomplishments shape where students complete their postsecondary credentials: within their high school region, elsewhere in Minnesota, or outside the state.


Key Findings
Demographics

Economic Status: Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate within their home region (67.8% vs. 55.7%), while non-disadvantaged students showed greater mobility, more often graduating elsewhere in MN or out of state.
Race/Ethnicity: American Indian (67.8%) and Hispanic (63.6%) graduates were most likely to stay in-region, while Asian/PI graduates were the least likely (48.7%), with higher rates graduating elsewhere in MN or out of state. White graduates showed a balanced pattern.
Special Education Status: Students with special education status were overwhelmingly more likely to remain in-region (73.8%) than non-special education students (57.7%), who were more mobile across the state and beyond.

High School Characteristics

School Locale: Rural graduates were less likely to remain in-region (38%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in MN, while mixed/urban graduates were more likely to stay local (56–61%).
Economic Conditions: Students from lower-unemployment, higher-wage areas were more likely to graduate in their home region or outside the state, while those from higher-unemployment, lower-wage areas were more likely to complete elsewhere in Minnesota. Effects were modest but consistent.

High School Accomplishments

Academic Achievement (ACT & MCA scores): Students with higher ACT and MCA scores were significantly more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. Lower-scoring students were more likely to remain in-region.
PSEO Participation: Participants were more geographically mobile, with higher rates of completing elsewhere in Minnesota or outside the state, while non-participants were more likely to stay local.
CTE Engagement: Students with deeper CTE involvement (more courses, concentrator/completor status) were far more likely to graduate in-region, while students with little or no CTE experience showed greater mobility.




Overall Conclusion
Tier 3 results show that geographic mobility in postsecondary completion is closely tied to academic strength, program participation, and demographics.

Students who are academically stronger or PSEO participants are more likely to graduate away from their home region, either elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state.
Students who are economically disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, or in special education, as well as those with deeper CTE engagement, are more likely to remain local.
Community economic conditions and school locale play smaller but notable roles, with rural and lower-wage contexts reinforcing regional completion.

In sum, Tier 3 highlights a divide between mobile, academically prepared students who pursue credentials beyond their home region, and students facing structural or programmatic constraints who are more likely to complete locally. This underscores the importance of academic preparation, resource access, and program opportunities in shaping not just whether students succeed in postsecondary, but where they do so.



Demographics
Key Findings:

Economic Status: Cramer’s V = 0.104, p < .001. Economically disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate within their high school region (67.8% vs. 55.7%), while non-disadvantaged students were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota (25.8% vs. 19.9%) or outside the state (18.5% vs. 12.3%).
Race/Ethnicity: Cramer’s V = 0.051, p < .001. American Indian (67.8%) and Hispanic (63.6%) graduates were most likely to remain in-region, while Asian/PI graduates were the least likely (48.7%), with higher rates completing elsewhere in MN (30.5%) or outside MN (20.8%). White graduates showed balanced outcomes across regions.
Special Education Status: Cramer’s V = 0.072, p < .001. Students with special education status were far more likely to remain in their high school region (73.8% vs. 57.7%), while non-special education students were more likely to complete elsewhere in MN (24.9% vs. 14.8%) or outside the state (17.4% vs. 11.4%).

Conclusion:
Demographic characteristics modestly influence the location of postsecondary graduation. Economically disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, and special education students are more likely to stay within their home region, reflecting limited geographic mobility. In contrast, non-disadvantaged, White, and Asian/PI students show greater mobility, more often completing their credentials elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. These differences suggest that resources, community ties, and support needs shape students’ ability or decision to pursue postsecondary opportunities beyond their home region.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Characteristics
Key Findings:

School Locale (Dem_Desc): Cramer’s V = 0.113, p < .001. Graduates from entirely rural schools were less likely to remain in-region (38%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota (49.3%). Graduates from town/rural mix (55.9%) and urban/town/rural mix schools (61%) were more likely to stay in-region.
Average Unemployment Rate: F(2, 18642) = 19.17, p < .001. Graduates from lower-unemployment areas were slightly more likely to graduate in their home region or outside Minnesota, while graduates from higher-unemployment areas were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota.
Average Wages (as % of State Average): F(2, 18642) = 107.57, p < .001. Students from higher-wage areas were more likely to graduate either in their home region or outside the state, while those from lower-wage areas were more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota.

Conclusion:
High school contextual characteristics exert a modest influence on where students complete postsecondary credentials. Locale matters somewhat, with rural students more likely to leave their region for other Minnesota institutions, while mixed/urban students are more likely to remain local. Economic conditions also play a role: students from stronger labor markets (lower unemployment, higher wages) are more likely to complete either locally or out of state, whereas weaker labor markets are tied to completion elsewhere in Minnesota. These effects are consistent but modest compared to demographic and accomplishment-based factors.

Key Findings:
Chi-square = 472.32, Cramer’s V = 0.113, p < .001. Graduation location varied modestly by school locale:

Entirely rural graduates were more likely to complete outside their region (49.3% elsewhere in MN, 12.6% outside MN). Only 38% stayed within their high school region.
Town/rural mix graduates were much more likely to stay in-region (55.9%) and less likely to go outside the state (15.4%).
Urban/town/rural mix graduates were the most likely to remain in-region (61%) and the most likely to graduate outside MN (17.9%), with relatively fewer moving elsewhere in MN (21%).

Conclusion:
School locale shows a modest association with where students graduate from postsecondary institutions. Graduates from entirely rural schools are less likely to remain in-region and more likely to move elsewhere in Minnesota, while graduates from mixed or urban/town/rural schools are more likely to complete within their home region. These findings suggest that regional school context modestly shapes geographic mobility after high school graduation.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
High School Accomplishments
Key Findings:

ACT Composite Score: F(2, 14470) = 536.91, p < .001. Students who graduated elsewhere in Minnesota had the highest ACT scores, while those who graduated in-region or outside Minnesota had lower scores.
PSEO Participation: Cramer’s V = 0.117, p < .001. PSEO participants were more geographically mobile—less likely to graduate in-region (54% vs. 66%) and more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or outside the state.
CTE Achievement: Cramer’s V = 0.068, p < .001. CTE concentrators/completors were the most likely to remain in their high school region (65.8%) and the least likely to graduate outside MN (13.2%). Non-CTE students were the least likely to stay local and the most likely to graduate out of state.
Total CTE Courses Taken: F(2, 18642) = 63.26, p < .001. Students who stayed in-region had taken the most CTE courses, while those who graduated elsewhere in MN or out of state had taken fewer.
MCA Math: F(2, 18435) = 204.54, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower math scores than those who graduated elsewhere in MN or out of state.
MCA Reading: F(2, 18346) = 156.66, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower reading scores than elsewhere-in-MN and out-of-state graduates.
MCA Science: F(2, 14864) = 236.46, p < .001. Region graduates had significantly lower science scores than both elsewhere-in-MN and out-of-state graduates.

Conclusion:
High school accomplishments are strongly associated with postsecondary graduation location. Higher academic achievement (ACT and MCA scores) is linked to greater geographic mobility, with stronger students more likely to graduate elsewhere in Minnesota or out of state. PSEO participation also increases mobility, while CTE engagement (more courses and concentrator/completor status) anchors students closer to home, with higher rates of in-region graduation. Overall, academic strength and dual-enrollment experiences encourage mobility, while CTE pathways reinforce regional ties.

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Tier 1: Core Access and Attainment

Demographics were the strongest and most consistent predictors. Economic disadvantage, race/ethnicity (especially American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students), and special education status all reduced likelihood of enrollment, attendance, and completion.
High School Characteristics (locale, local unemployment, wages) had weak and inconsistent effects.
High School Accomplishments were powerful predictors. Higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO participation strongly boosted immediate enrollment, persistence, and graduation. In contrast, greater CTE engagement was associated with lower enrollment and graduation, aligning with workforce entry rather than postsecondary continuation.

title: Post-secondary pathways
section: Tier 2: Type of Postsecondary Experience (Highest Credential Earned)
text:
Tier 2: Type of Postsecondary Experience (Highest Credential Earned)

Economic disadvantage and special education status created the steepest barriers to earning a bachelor’s or higher degree, with these groups concentrated in “Some college” or sub-associate credentials.
Racial disparities persisted: White and Asian/PI students were far more likely to complete bachelor’s or graduate degrees, while American Indian, Black, and Hispanic students were more likely to stop at associate’s or leave with no credential.
Academic readiness and PSEO participation were the strongest positive predictors of bachelor’s+ attainment. Students with higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO experience were much more likely to progress to advanced credentials.
CTE engagement again tracked with sub-baccalaureate attainment, with concentrators/completors more likely to finish with associate’s or stop at “Some college.”

title: Post-secondary pathways
text:
Tier 3: Location of Postsecondary Graduation

Demographics shaped mobility: disadvantaged, American Indian, Hispanic, and special education students were most likely to graduate within their high school region, while non-disadvantaged, White, and Asian/PI students showed greater mobility (elsewhere in MN or out-of-state).
High school characteristics mattered modestly. Rural students tended to leave their region but stay within Minnesota, while students from stronger labor markets (lower unemployment, higher wages) were more likely to graduate in-region or out-of-state.
Accomplishments mattered most: Higher ACT/MCA scores and PSEO participation were strongly tied to graduating outside the home region, while heavier CTE engagement (more courses, concentrator/completor status) was associated with staying local.

The dataset now has 211,008 instances that provide a number of characteristics about an individuals enrollment.
My goal is to end up with a dataset where each observation (row) represents a unique (unduplicated) individual that’s tied to the school from which they graduated. Here’s how I will do that.

PersonID: change to integer
K12OrganizationID: change to integer.
K12EnrTimeID: Change so it’s only the year
Grade: eliminate - unimportant since we are mostly concerned about whether they graduated.
EconomicStatusIndicator: I will change this to two categories. Whether they were ever eligible for reduce priced or free meal will be coded as 1 (eligible = codes 1, 2, 4, 5) at any point in the dataset. The remaining will be coded as 0.
FederalRaceIndicator: eliminate - I’m going to use the RaceEthnicity column instead.
PSEO columns: I’m most concerned about whether they participated in PSEO or not. A new column will be created indicated whether there was a “Y” coded for either the “PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator” or “PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator” columns at any point in the dataset. The two original columns will be eliminated.
StatusEnd: I will only include individuals that have StatusEnd coded as an 8 or 9.
Gender: included and not changed.
SpecialEdStatus: I will split this into two categories. The first is that a student did not require special education services (codes 1-2) at any point in the dataset. The other category will be that they require special education (codes 4 - 9) at any point in the dataset.
Limited English: keep with no changes.
Primary language: I’m going to create two categories. One being that English is the primary language while the other will be that English is NOT the primary language at any point in the dataset.
Homeless: Keep with no changes.

We first need to create a list of all individuals with the StatusEnd code of 8 or 9 (graduated). In addition, we need to remove any student that graduated before 2008. This is because we will not have their full Sophmore - Senior records which is especially important when attempting to identify whether the number of CTE courses taken predicts migration.
The other element I want to add is a pre-covid and post-covid variable. All individuals whose grad year is before 2020 will be labeled pre-covid and all others wil lbe post-covid.
This “graduates list” will be the list on which we will bind all the other variables.


graduates <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  filter(StatusEnd %in% c(8,9)) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4),
         grad.year = as.integer(grad.year),
         grad.year.covid = ifelse(grad.year > 2019, "Post-covid grad", "Pre-covid grad")) %>%
  select(PersonID, K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, grad.year, grad.year.covid, Gender, LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator, HomelessIndicator, county.name, countyfp, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2007) 


Next we need to create new columns for the variables that will indicate a certain status has been met at any point in the dataset for each PersonID. For example, we want a column that indicates a PersonID was enrolled in PSEO at some point in the dataset. The variables that need a new column created are;

EconomicStatusIndicator
PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator & PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator
SpecialEdStatus
HomeprimaryLanguage



# Lets start with economic status indicator
k12.enr.esi.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, EconomicStatusIndicator) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(economic.status.code = ifelse(EconomicStatusIndicator %in% c(1,2,4,5), 1, 0),
         economic.status.code.sum = sum(economic.status.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(economic.status = ifelse(economic.status.code.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, economic.status)

# PSEO

k12.enr.pseo.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne%>%
  select(PersonID, PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator, PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator) %>%
  mutate(PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator = ifelse(PostSecondaryEnrollmentOptionsIndicator == "Y", 1, 0),
         PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator = ifelse(PSEOConcurrentEnrollmentIndicator == "Y", 1, 0)) %>%
  gather(key = "pseo.type", value = "indicator", 2:3) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(pseo = sum(indicator)) %>%
  mutate(pseo.participant = ifelse(pseo > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, pseo.participant)

# Special Ed status

k12.enr.spced.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, SpecialEdStatus) %>%
  mutate(SpecialEdStatus.code = ifelse(SpecialEdStatus %in% c(4,5,6,7,8,9), 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(SpecialEdStatus.sum = sum(SpecialEdStatus.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(SpecialEdStatus = ifelse(SpecialEdStatus.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, SpecialEdStatus)

# Home Primary Language

k12.enr.homeprimlang.indicator <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, HomePrimaryLanguage) %>%
  mutate(HomePrimaryLanguage.code = ifelse(HomePrimaryLanguage == 11, 0, 1)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(HomePrimaryLanguage.sum = sum(HomePrimaryLanguage.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(non.english.home = ifelse(HomePrimaryLanguage.sum > 0, 1, 0)) %>%
  select(PersonID, non.english.home)

# Race

k12.enr.race <- enrollment.org.ne %>%
  select(PersonID, RaceEthnicity) %>%
  mutate(RaceEthnicity = ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 0, "Unknown",
                                ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 1, "AI",
                                       ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 2, "Asian/PI",
                                              ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 3, "Hispanic",
                                                     ifelse(RaceEthnicity == 4, "Black", "White"))))),
         RaceEthnicity = as.factor(RaceEthnicity)) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, RaceEthnicity) %>%
  mutate(code = ifelse(RaceEthnicity == "Unknown", 0, 1)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(code == max(code)) %>%
  ungroup %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID, RaceEthnicity)


Now we can combine the list of graduates with the status indicators.


k12.enrollment.master <- graduates %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.esi.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.pseo.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.spced.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.homeprimlang.indicator, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(k12.enr.race, by = "PersonID") %>%
  select(PersonID, K12OrganizationID, OrganizationName, county.name, countyfp, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region, grad.year, grad.year.covid, Gender, LimitedEnglishProficiencyIndicator, HomelessIndicator, economic.status, pseo.participant, SpecialEdStatus, non.english.home, RaceEthnicity)

title: Local Employment CART Analysis
text:
Comparative Summary
Year 1 after Graduation
At one year, regional economic conditions dominate. Graduates from counties with lower wages (<82% of state average) are most likely to remain employed in their high school region. Academic factors refine this: students with moderate MCA Math and ACT scores are more anchored locally, while those with very high ACT scores are somewhat more mobile. Rural students are also more likely to stay, unless high academic performance gives them the credentials to pursue opportunities elsewhere. Overall, weaker local economies and moderate academic preparation are the clearest anchors to early regional employment.
Year 5 after Graduation
By five years, postsecondary pathways replace high school characteristics as the main anchors. Graduates who complete college in their home region are the most likely to stay employed there. Those who attend institutions outside the region (even within Minnesota) or who do not graduate are much more likely to work elsewhere. Local labor markets still matter: when wages are low and unemployment is high, graduates are more likely to remain in their home region. Moderate ACT scores and credential attainment reinforce anchoring, while strong labor markets elsewhere and higher ACT performance increase mobility.
Year 10 after Graduation
A decade after high school, educational attainment and place of graduation remain decisive. Graduates who earned postsecondary credentials in their home region, especially bachelor’s degrees, are strongly tied to local employment. In contrast, those who graduated outside the region (even elsewhere in Minnesota) are less likely to return. ACT scores become more important over time: very high scorers are the most mobile, while moderate scorers remain anchored. Community context continues to shape retention — graduates from rural and town/rural areas are more likely to stay, while urban graduates are more mobile. Weaker local wages reinforce anchoring, while stronger wages encourage outward mobility.
Conclusion
Across all time horizons, meaningful employment in the region is the dominant outcome. What changes over time are the anchors:

In the short term, it is local economic conditions (low wages, rural context).
By the mid-term, it is postsecondary completion in the home region.
In the long term, it is a combination of regional college graduation, rural upbringing, and moderate academic achievement that keeps graduates rooted, while high academic performance and education outside the region drive mobility.

The consistent message is that place of postsecondary education and community context are central levers. Strengthening local higher education pathways, especially those tied to rural areas, and ensuring accessible, high-quality employment opportunities in weaker wage markets, are the clearest policy solutions to reinforce regional workforce retention.
