sat.taken

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the SAT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 228.74, Cramer’s V = 0.070, p < .001, N = 46,777【595†source】
5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 188.76, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 34,683【596†source】
10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 99.99, Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001, N = 19,828【597†source】

The effect sizes are small but consistent. The key pattern is that SAT takers are far more likely to attend postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: SAT takers are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (73.5% vs. 47.3% for non‑takers). Regional meaningful employment is much lower for SAT takers (3.2% vs. 15.5%), while disconnection is also somewhat lower (9.0% vs. 11.7%)【595†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: SAT takers maintain higher postsecondary enrollment (30.1% vs. 15.8%). Regional meaningful employment is still much lower (7.6% vs. 26.8%). Interestingly, SAT takers are slightly more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (18.2% vs. 15.1%). Disconnection is higher among SAT takers (28.6% vs. 20.9%)【596†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: SAT takers continue to show very low regional meaningful employment (11.5% vs. 29.5%), while statewide meaningful employment is similar (18.6% vs. 19.4%). Disconnection is much higher among SAT takers (55.9% vs. 32.0%)【597†source】.
Overall, SAT participation identifies a small group of students who overwhelmingly pursue postsecondary initially, but long‑term outcomes show weak regional attachment and much higher disconnection, suggesting that SAT takers may be more mobile, pursue opportunities outside the region or state, or leave tracked employment systems altogether.

MCA.R

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Reading scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42500) = 689.45, p < .001
5 years after graduation: F(4, 31013) = 119.45, p < .001
10 years after graduation: F(3, 17590) = 237.15, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant over time. The primary pattern is that higher MCA Reading scores are associated with postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are more tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful/disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:

Postsecondary attendees score about +0.26 higher than regional meaningful workers (p < .001).
Not meaningful (+0.09) and No MN record (+0.14) also score higher than regional meaningful (p ≤ .02).
Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is linked to lower reading scores, while higher scores track into postsecondary and other categories.

Year 5:

Postsecondary (+0.21), statewide meaningful (+0.17), and No MN record (+0.08) all score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
Not meaningful scores slightly below regional meaningful (−0.17, p < .001).
Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment sits lower on the MCA-R spectrum, while postsecondary and statewide jobs skew higher.

Year 10:

Statewide meaningful (+0.18) and No MN record (+0.14) are significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
Not meaningful scores considerably lower (−0.25, p < .001).
Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains tied to lower MCA-R scores, with higher scores concentrated in statewide meaningful employment or outside tracked records.

Overall, MCA Reading reinforces that academic achievement predicts longer-term educational and statewide work pathways, while lower scores are associated with stronger regional attachment but also greater risk of not meaningful outcomes.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
MCA.S

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Science scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 37501) = 544.02, p < .001
5 years after graduation: F(4, 26050) = 160.29, p < .001
10 years after graduation: F(3, 11879) = 81.74, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant through 10 years. The key pattern is that higher MCA Science scores are associated with postsecondary education and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:

Postsecondary attendees score substantially higher than regional meaningful (+0.38, p < .001).
Statewide meaningful (+0.07) also scores higher than regional meaningful (p = .025).
Not meaningful (−0.07) and No MN record (−0.12) score below postsecondary.
Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful work is tied to lower MCA-S scores, while education and statewide jobs are tied to higher scores.

Year 5:

Statewide meaningful (+0.25) and postsecondary (+0.32) are far above regional meaningful (p < .001).
No MN record (+0.11) is also higher.
Not meaningful (−0.04) is slightly below regional meaningful (p = .044).
Takeaway: by 5 years, the gap widens, with statewide and postsecondary pathways clearly tied to higher MCA-S scores, while regional meaningful remains lower.

Year 10:

Statewide meaningful (+0.27) and No MN record (+0.18) score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
Not meaningful (−0.31) scores well below regional meaningful (p < .001).
Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower MCA-S scores, while higher scores push students into statewide jobs or out of tracked MN employment.

Overall, MCA Science mirrors the MCA Reading pattern: academic achievement is strongly tied to educational and statewide pathways, while lower achievement is associated with stronger regional attachment or risk of weaker employment outcomes.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
MCA.M

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Math scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42550) = 1344.53, p < .001
5 years after graduation: F(4, 33107) = 152.39, p < .001
10 years after graduation: F(3, 18728) = 94.98, p < .001

The results show an especially strong relationship in the first year, with effects tapering but still significant through Year 10. The key pattern is that higher MCA Math scores are linked to postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment and weaker outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:

Postsecondary attendees score much higher than regional meaningful (+0.58, p < .001).
Statewide meaningful is also above regional meaningful (+0.07, p = .026).
Not meaningful (−0.06) and No MN record (−0.17) score lower than regional meaningful (p ≤ .001).
Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful employment is positioned between low‑scoring disconnected outcomes and high‑scoring education pathways.

Year 5:

Postsecondary (+0.28) and statewide meaningful (+0.27) both score significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
Not meaningful (−0.08) and No MN record (−0.24) score below regional meaningful (p < .001).
Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful work is associated with lower scores relative to statewide and postsecondary, but still stronger than disconnected categories.

Year 10:

Statewide meaningful (+0.29) remains higher than regional meaningful (p < .001).
No MN record shows a mixed pattern: one contrast indicates higher scores (+0.13, p < .001) while another shows lower scores (−0.15, p < .001), reflecting sub‑patterns in this group.
Not meaningful (−0.10 to −0.38) scores consistently lower than regional meaningful (p < .001).
Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful jobs remain linked to mid‑range math scores, lower than statewide/postsecondary but higher than disconnected outcomes.

Overall, MCA Math reinforces the trend seen in other MCA measures: higher achievement channels students into education and statewide employment, while regional meaningful employment is associated with lower but not the lowest scores, positioning it as a middle pathway.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
cte.achievement

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between CTE achievement (Concentrator/Completer, Participant, No CTE) and post‑graduation outcomes across all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 508.14, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 46,777【663†source】
5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 307.50, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 34,683【664†source】
10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 174.53, Cramer’s V = 0.066, p < .001, N = 19,828【665†source】

The associations are modest but consistent. The clearest relationship is that CTE Concentrators/Completers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while students with no CTE are more likely to be in postsecondary or outside regional attachment.


Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for CTE Concentrators/Completers (19.4%), compared to Participants (15.1%) and No CTE students (12.6%). Postsecondary enrollment is much higher among No CTE (51.3%) and Participants (49.2%) than Concentrators/Completers (41.5%). This suggests that CTE pathways steer students more quickly into regional work while non‑CTE students delay employment through postsecondary【663†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: The regional employment gap persists: 31.9% for Concentrators/Completers vs. 27.2% for Participants and 22.9% for No CTE. Postsecondary attendance is relatively low across all groups (13–17%), but still higher for those without CTE. Concentrators/Completers maintain stronger local employment connections, while non‑CTE students lean slightly more toward statewide employment (15.7%)【664†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains strongest among Concentrators/Completers (34.6%), compared to Participants (29.1%) and No CTE students (25.5%). Statewide meaningful employment is more evenly distributed, while disconnection is highest among those with No CTE (35.5%). The long‑term pattern confirms that CTE achievement reinforces regional employment pathways, while students outside CTE are more likely to leave the region or experience disconnection【665†source】.
Overall, CTE achievement consistently predicts stronger regional workforce attachment, distinguishing Concentrators/Completers as the group most likely to remain engaged in meaningful employment within the region over time.

total.cte.courses.taken

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the number of CTE courses taken and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 45696) = 232.40, p < .001
5 years after graduation: F(4, 33828) = 104.15, p < .001
10 years after graduation: F(3, 19320) = 36.17, p < .001

The results show a consistent pattern: students who took more CTE courses are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment, while students with fewer CTE courses lean toward postsecondary, statewide, or disconnected pathways.


Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:

Regional meaningful employment is associated with higher CTE course counts compared to postsecondary (−0.72, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.21, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.37, p < .001).
Postsecondary students have the lowest CTE course counts, confirming that heavier CTE load ties directly into early regional work.

Year 5:

Regional meaningful again shows higher CTE courses than postsecondary (−0.61, p < .001), meaningful MN (−0.44, p < .001), not meaningful (−0.33, p < .001), and no MN record (−0.45, p < .001).
Postsecondary and statewide workers come from lower CTE course backgrounds.
Takeaway: at five years, regional meaningful work is strongly linked to CTE engagement, while those with fewer CTE courses are dispersed across statewide or disconnected outcomes.

Year 10:

Regional meaningful still has higher CTE courses compared to statewide meaningful (−0.31, p < .001) and no MN record (−0.31, p < .001).
Not meaningful outcomes also show slightly higher CTE courses than regional (+0.21, p < .001), reflecting a mixed subgroup.
Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment is still concentrated among heavier CTE participants, reinforcing CTE as a strong predictor of regional attachment.

Overall, total CTE course load demonstrates that increased CTE participation anchors students more firmly in regional employment, while lighter CTE engagement is linked to education and broader employment pathways.

Key Patterns & Comparative Insights
Strongest Associations

The attendance variables (attended within 1st year, ever attended) and postsecondary graduation have the strongest early associations, with Cramer’s V values above 0.5–0.6 at Year 1. These measures clearly separate students who pursue higher education from those who do not, with PS attenders/graduates far less likely to enter immediate regional work but more likely to gain stable employment outcomes over time.
Highest credential level also shows strong early differentiation, with higher credentials linked to delayed workforce entry and eventual statewide mobility, while lower or mid‑level credentials tie more closely to regional jobs.

Moderate Associations

PS graduation location and institution sector matter less than attendance or graduation itself but still provide meaningful distinctions. Regional PS graduates are far more likely to remain in local employment, while graduates from 4‑year universities or from outside the region show greater statewide mobility.

Regional Employment Predictors

Non‑attenders and non‑graduates are consistently more likely to enter regional meaningful employment early, but they also carry much higher risks of disconnection in the long run.
CTE‑like pathways within postsecondary (2‑year institutions, Associate degrees, regional institutions) show the strongest alignment with long‑term regional workforce attachment.
Bachelor’s+ degrees, 4‑year universities, and graduation outside MN are consistently tied to statewide employment and mobility, reducing regional anchoring.

Overall Insight
Postsecondary experiences draw a clear line between regional anchoring vs. statewide mobility.

Access and completion of postsecondary education lead to broader statewide opportunities and reduced risk of disconnection.
Absence of postsecondary pathways results in earlier regional employment but higher long‑term vulnerability.
The type, level, and location of postsecondary attainment nuance this divide: regional and 2‑year pathways strengthen local attachment, while higher‑level and out‑of‑region pathways expand opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending postsecondary within the first year after high school and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 27,442.69, Cramer’s V = 0.542, p < .001, N = 46,777【712†source】
5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 4,207.23, Cramer’s V = 0.246, p < .001, N = 34,683【713†source】
10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 408.26, Cramer’s V = 0.101, p < .001, N = 19,828【714†source】

The effect is extremely strong in the first year and weakens over time, though it remains statistically significant. The main pattern is that students who attend PS within the first year are much less likely to be in regional meaningful employment, while those who do not attend are far more likely to start working in the region.


Interpretation Over Time

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1,030.86, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 19,828【762†source】

The association is strong in the first year, moderates by year 5, and weakens further by year 10, though it remains significant. The key distinction is that higher credentials (Bachelor’s or above) delay regional employment but lead to stronger statewide employment later, while lower or mid‑level credentials (Associate, less than Associate) are more tied to early and sustained regional employment.


Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students with no college are most likely to be in regional meaningful employment (19.9%), but also heavily represented in disconnection categories (44.2% not meaningful, 30.1% no record). Those with some college or Associate degrees show moderate regional employment (18–19%) but are strongly concentrated in “attending PS” (49–69%). Students pursuing a Bachelor’s or higher overwhelmingly remain in education (86.5%) and show the lowest regional employment (5.7%)【760†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment peaks among less than Associate (42.3%) and Associate degree earners (36.5%), with some college also relatively strong (29.2%). By contrast, Bachelor’s or higher show lower regional attachment (19.1%) but higher statewide meaningful employment (20.5%). Non‑college individuals still show significant disconnection (27.4% not meaningful, 37.0% no record)【761†source】.
Year 10: The regional advantage of Associate and sub‑Associate credentials remains high (42–43%), while Bachelor’s or higher show stronger statewide employment (27.9%) and lower regional employment (26.5%). Non‑college individuals continue to show the weakest outcomes, with the highest disconnection rates (41.7% no record)【762†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that mid‑level credentials (Associate and below) strongly anchor individuals in regional employment, while Bachelor’s and above foster statewide mobility and stronger longer‑term outcomes, and no credential consistently yields the weakest employment stability.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
ps.grad.location

Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between location of postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(9) = 2713.62, Cramer’s V = 0.197, p < .001, N = 23,341【772†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 3699.62, Cramer’s V = 0.207, p < .001, N = 28,840【773†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 1609.04, Cramer’s V =0.164, p < .001, N = 19,827【774†source】

The association is moderate in years 1 and 5 and slightly weaker by year 10. The central divide is that regional PS graduates are consistently more likely to work in the region, while graduates outside MN or at MN institutions outside the region are more likely to pursue statewide or out‑of‑state pathways.


Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Regional graduates show the strongest immediate tie to local jobs, with 65.8% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 23.8% of non‑graduates, 28.7% of MN graduates outside the region, and 22.0% of graduates outside MN. Non‑graduates are most often disconnected (43.4% “not meaningful” and 25.9% “no record”)【772†source】.
Year 5: Regional graduates remain highly concentrated in regional employment (50.2%), far above MN graduates outside the region (18.3%) or graduates outside MN (20.4%). By contrast, MN graduates outside the region have the highest statewide employment (44.0%), reflecting mobility within the state. Non‑graduates remain more disconnected (28.4% “not meaningful” and 31.0% “no record”)【773†source】.
Year 10: Regional graduates sustain a long‑term edge in local employment (43.1%), while MN graduates outside the region remain more mobile (38.0% in statewide employment). Graduates outside MN have lower regional (20.7%) and statewide (17.8%) employment, with a higher share of disconnection (49.4% “no record”). Non‑graduates remain the weakest group, with only 25.6% regional employment and the highest share of disconnection (36.7% “no record”)【774†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that regional PS graduation strongly anchors individuals in the local workforce, while graduation outside the region or outside MN promotes mobility and statewide attachment. Non‑graduates remain at the greatest risk of disconnection across all timeframes.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
Key Patterns & Comparative Insights

Demographics

SpecialEd Status and Race/Ethnicity stand out as the strongest demographic predictors, particularly in shaping early outcomes.
Gender, Economic Status, and English Learner status show weaker associations that fade quickly.
Overall, demographics set context but are less determinative compared to later factors.



High School Characteristics

Local context (rural/urban, unemployment, wage levels) influences early pathways, especially pushing some students into immediate work.
These effects diminish with time, suggesting that structural local factors matter most at the point of high school exit, but individual choices and credentials overtake them later.



High School Accomplishments

Clear split between academic and technical tracks:

College-prep measures (ACT, PSEO, MCA, AP, SAT) → lead to postsecondary and statewide employment, reducing regional attachment.
CTE measures (CTE achievement, total courses) → tie directly to regional meaningful employment, with effects persisting 10 years out.

MCA Math in particular emerges as the strongest achievement predictor across all accomplishment variables.



Postsecondary Experiences

This is the most powerful section overall. Postsecondary attendance and completion dominate long-term outcomes.
Attenders and graduates show stronger statewide and stable employment, while non-attenders and non-graduates enter regional jobs early but face greater disconnection risk long-term.
Institution type, credential level, and location add nuance:

Regional and 2-year pathways → strengthen regional attachment.
4-year and out-of-state pathways → expand statewide opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Local Employment Cross-tabs
text:
Overall Conclusion
Across all sections, a consistent theme emerges:

Regional meaningful employment is most strongly predicted by career/technical education in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.
Statewide meaningful employment and mobility are driven by academic achievement, 4-year college pathways, and higher credentials.
Disconnection is most common among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker academic/CTE preparation, compounded by local economic stressors.

In sum, the evidence highlights two diverging but equally important pathways:

Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
CTE + regional PS pathways → stronger anchoring in the regional workforce.

Both play vital roles in shaping the Northeast Minnesota labor market and should be considered complementary in policy and planning.

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Post-pruning
The idea here is to allow the decision tree to grow fully and observe the CP value. There are two methods for identifying the CP code;

Use the cp value with the lowest xerror from the base model.
Use the cp value with the next lowest xerror that is within the standard error.



cp_table <- ps.grad.location.model.preprune$cptable

min_xerror <- min(cp_table[, "xerror"])
min_xerror_se <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[,"xerror"]), "xstd"]

threshold <- min_xerror + min_xerror_se

one_se_index <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= threshold)[1] 

cp_1se <- cp_table[one_se_index, "CP"]

optimal_cp <- ps.grad.location.model.preprune$cptable[which.min(ps.grad.location.model.preprune$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]


# Prune the hr_base_model based on the optimal cp value

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Main takeaway
Model Performance
The post-pruned tree achieved 61.5% accuracy with a root node error of 42.5%. While not extremely high, this accuracy reflects a meaningful improvement over baseline and demonstrates that a small set of predictors can capture important patterns in postsecondary graduation location.
Key Predictors
The most influential predictors retained after pruning were:

ACT Composite Score
Economic Status
Race/Ethnicity
Took ACT

Interpretation of Tree Structure
Graduation from a regional postsecondary institution was most strongly linked with higher ACT scores (≥28). Students demonstrating strong academic preparation were more likely to complete a credential in their home region. This pattern was especially pronounced among those from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, suggesting that high-achieving, low-income students often pursued regional options rather than leaving the area.
By contrast, students with low ACT scores (<20) or who did not take the ACT were much more likely to not graduate at all. Students with mid-range ACT performance and less clear demographic ties (e.g., race/ethnicity unknown) were more likely to graduate outside the region.
Summary
The CART model indicates that high academic readiness is the strongest pathway into regional postsecondary graduation, particularly when paired with economic disadvantage. In other words, the students most anchored to regional institutions were those who combined strong academic performance with fewer economic resources. This suggests that regional colleges play an especially important role in providing access and opportunity for capable but economically constrained students, while lower academic readiness often foreclosed postsecondary completion altogether.

title: Post-secondary Paths CART
text:
Main takeaway
Model Performance
The pre-pruned CART model achieved an accuracy of 65.9%, with a root node error of 42.5%. This represents a solid improvement over baseline and indicates that a small set of academic and demographic factors predict credential attainment reasonably well.
Key Predictors
The most influential predictors retained were:

ACT Composite Score
Economic Status
Race/Ethnicity
Took ACT

Interpretation of Tree Structure
Completion of a bachelor’s degree or higher was most strongly linked to taking the ACT and achieving a score of at least 21. Students from across racial/ethnic groups with higher ACT scores, particularly those without economic disadvantage, were the most likely to attain these higher-level credentials.
Students with low ACT scores (<21), or who did not take the ACT at all, were most likely to not graduate postsecondary. Economic status compounded this effect, with disadvantaged students at greater risk of non-completion even when they had moderate ACT scores.
Although the tree did not form a distinct pathway that isolated associate degrees or lower, these outcomes generally clustered among students with mid-range ACT scores (21–24). Within this range, students with some academic preparation but lower overall scores were less competitive for bachelor’s pathways but still positioned to complete sub-baccalaureate programs. Economic disadvantage increased the likelihood of falling short of a bachelor’s degree, which in many cases meant completing an associate degree or certificate instead of leaving without any credential.
Summary
The CART model highlights three general pathways:

Strong ACT performance (≥21), no economic disadvantage → bachelor’s degree or higher
Mid-range ACT performance, especially with disadvantage → associate degree or lower
Low or no ACT performance (<21 or no test) → non-completion

In other words, sub-baccalaureate completion emerges as a “middle pathway,” tied to moderate academic readiness and shaped by socioeconomic constraints. Students without strong academic signals often fail to complete, while those with higher scores move into bachelor’s attainment. The associate/certificate route, while less cleanly predicted in the tree, reflects a mix of opportunity and constraint: it anchors students with some preparation, but often limited resources, into shorter credentials that still provide local labor market value.

Summary of SAT data
Lets check to see what percentage of the master dataset has taken the SAT.
There is a tiny percentage of the dataset that has taken the SAT, 1.7%. With this information I don’t see a need to check whether there is a significant difference in students taking the SAT based on RUCA category or County. Even if there is a significant difference, there just isn’t enough observations to make a difference.


sat.total <- master.8 %>%
  group_by(sat.taken) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(sat.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 0:1))))  %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, digits = 0, "")

title: Categorizing Range Schools
section: Primary Iron Range School Districts (Core Iron Range)
text:
Primary Iron Range School Districts (Core Iron Range)
These are located directly within the Mesabi Iron Range and are almost always considered part of it:

Rock Ridge Public Schools (ISD 2909) – Formed by the merger of Virginia and Eveleth-Gilbert district
Mountain Iron-Buhl (ISD 712)
Chisholm (ISD 695)
Hibbing (ISD 701)
Nashwauk-Keewatin (ISD 319)
Ely (ISD 696)
Mesabi East (ISD 2711) – Based in Aurora, serving Aurora, Hoyt Lakes, and Biwabik.

title: Categorizing Range Schools
section: Borderline or Secondary Iron Range School Districts
text:
Borderline or Secondary Iron Range School Districts
These districts are near the Iron Range and are sometimes included depending on the context:

Cook County (ISD 166) – More North Shore than Iron Range, but very rural and sometimes lumped into broader regional definitions.
Northland Community Schools (ISD 118, in Remer) – Not on the Mesabi Range, but sometimes included in broader northeastern discussions.
Floodwood (ISD 698) – Located west of Duluth and near the southern edge of Iron Range influence.

Deer River (ISD 317) – South and west of Grand Rapids; sometimes considered part of the western fringe.
Grand Rapids (ISD 318) – A larger hub district west of the traditional range; sometimes included as a key service and economic center for the region.

title: Categorizing Range Schools
text:
Not Typically Considered Iron Range
These are nearby but not part of the Iron Range proper:

Duluth Public Schools (ISD 709) – Major city in NE MN, but culturally and economically separate from the Iron Range.
Two Harbors/Silver Bay (Lake Superior ISD 381) – On the North Shore.
Carlton, Cloquet, Moose Lake – More in the Carlton County area, not considered Iron Range.
International Falls (ISD 361) – Farther north, part of the borderlands, not the Range.

In the original dataset we have 1598552 rows and 16 columns. Below is a description of each variable.

Empl_TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
CalendarYear: Year
CalendarQuarter: Quarter within the year in which the data applies. Quarters are;

1 = Jan - Mar
2 = Apr - Jun
3 = Jul - Sep
4 = Oct - Dec

EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
IndustryID: Auto generated ID code for a record in the Industry dimension.
USIndustryCode: Six-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
GroupCode: Four-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
IndustryGroup: Definition of GroupCode variable, the 4-digit NAICS code
OwnershipCode: A classification system based upon the controlling interest of the establishment primarily designed to distinguish between governmental and non-governmental establishments

10 = Federal government
20 = State government
30 = Local government
50 = Private

EmployerLocationTotalWagesPaid: The total wages paid to all workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
QuarterlyAverageEmployment: The average number of workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
LocationID: ???
EconomicDevelopmentRegion: The 13 economic development regions within the state of Minnesota as defined by the Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED).

R01000 EDR 1 - Northwest

R02000 EDR 2 - Headwaters

R03000 EDR 3 - Arrowhead

R04000 EDR 4 - West Central

R05000 EDR 5 - North Central

R06E00 EDR 6E - Southwest Central

R06W00 EDR 6W - Upper Minnesota Valley

R07E00 EDR 7E - East Central

R07W00 EDR 7W - Central

R08000 EDR 8 - Southwest

R11000 EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities

EconomicDevelopmentRegionName: Name of EDR
County: Minnesota county code to which this institution belongs. This can be used as a foreign key into the Geography dimension on MNCounty.

Link to codes

CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.
MNCounty: County Code for this location as assigned by the state of Minnesota.

Link to codes City: All of the city data is NA



So all the previous datasets we structured and filtered so that each observation in the master dataset was an individual. We will want to continue to do the same. So we need to create an employment dataset with the following columns;

PersonID
High school graduation year
Whether the individual had an employment record the year of, and each subsequent year, of high school graduation.
How many years after graduation each employment check is (i.e. grad.year.1, grad.year.2,….etc.)





grad.years <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year)

mn.emp.record.year <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  mutate(mn.emp.record = "MN emp record") %>%
  filter(CalendarYear > 2007) %>%
  filter(CalendarYear < 2024) %>%
  complete(PersonID, CalendarYear, fill = list(mn.emp.record = "No MN emp record")) 

mn.emp.record <- grad.years %>%
  left_join(mn.emp.record.year, by = c("PersonID")) %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year, CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(-update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

The dataset above provides each unique PersonID from our master list along with each possible grad year and subsequent years (grad.year.0, grad.year.1, grad.year.2 … grad.year.11).
Here is the logic;

grad.year.x > 2023: mn.emp.record == “After 2023”,
if there’s a MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “MN emp record”
if there’s no MN employment record for the PersonID and the grad.year.x: mn.emp.record == “No MN emp record”

There are 797,056 rows in this dataset with 49,816 individuals.




The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2019, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.


emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(EconomicDevelopmentRegionName = edr) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.employer %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),

         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         update = ifelse(CalendarYear < hs.grad.year, "Not graduated HS", "Graduated")) %>%
  filter(update == "Graduated") %>%
  select(-update) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(grad.year.seq = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.year.seq) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(hs.grad.year, .direction = "down") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = ifelse(is.na(CalendarYear), hs.grad.year + (grad.year.seq - 1), CalendarYear),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", mn.emp.record),
         mn.emp.record = ifelse(is.na(mn.emp.record), "No MN emp record", mn.emp.record),
         grad.year = paste("grad.year.", grad.year.seq-1, sep = "")) %>%
  select(-grad.year.seq)

Here is the logic;

title: Employment states each year
text:
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
This will be a couple step process. First we will build a dataset that has each grad.year.x from each PersonID high school graduation year and match it with the MN employment records. We will end up with each PersonID having each grad.year.x along with wither they have a MN employment record, whether they had meaningful employment, whether grad.year.x is after 2019, or whether they have no MN employment record.


meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(AnnualHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11"),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(AnnualHoursWorked > 999, "Meaningful employment", mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(CalendarYear > 2023, "After 2023", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "MN emp record", "MN emp record - not meaningful", new.mn.emp.record),
         new.mn.emp.record = ifelse(mn.emp.record == "No MN emp record", "No MN emp record", new.mn.emp.record),
         meaningful.emp.code = ifelse(new.mn.emp.record == "Meaningful employment", 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, CalendarYear) %>%
  filter(meaningful.emp.code == max(meaningful.emp.code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, grad.year, meaningful.emp.code, .keep_all = TRUE)

Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.


emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(EconomicDevelopmentRegionName = edr) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),

         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),

  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.employer %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),

  select(-county.match) %>%
  rename(county.match = new.county.match) %>%
  mutate(edr.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.edr.match = ifelse(edr.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.edr == hs.edr, "Meaningful emp - match", edr.match),
         new.edr.match = ifelse(new.edr.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.edr.match),
         new.edr.match = fct_relevel(new.edr.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-edr.match) %>%
  rename(edr.match = new.edr.match) %>%
  mutate(region.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.region.match = ifelse(region.match == "Meaningful employment" & emp.pr %in% c("Northeast"), "Meaningful emp - match", region.match),
         new.region.match = ifelse(new.region.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.region.match),
         new.region.match = fct_relevel(new.region.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-region.match) %>%
  rename(region.match = new.region.match) %>%
  mutate(state.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.state.match = ifelse(!is.na(emp.edr) & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match",
                                  ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)" & state.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - match", state.match)),
         new.state.match = fct_relevel(new.state.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-state.match) %>%
  rename(state.match = new.state.match) %>%
  mutate(Dem_Desc.match = new.mn.emp.record,
         new.Dem_Desc.match = ifelse(Dem_Desc.match == "Meaningful employment" & hs.Dem_Desc == emp.Dem_Desc, "Meaningful emp - match", Dem_Desc.match),
         new.Dem_Desc.match = ifelse(new.Dem_Desc.match == "Meaningful employment", "Meaningful emp - no match", new.Dem_Desc.match),
         new.Dem_Desc.match = fct_relevel(new.Dem_Desc.match, "Meaningful emp - match", "Meaningful emp - no match", "MN emp record - not meaningful", "No MN emp record", "After 2023")) %>%
  select(-Dem_Desc.match) %>%
  rename(Dem_Desc.match = new.Dem_Desc.match) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, grad.year, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year, grad.year, county.match, edr.match, region.match, Dem_Desc.match, state.match)

This dataset has 26,130 rows and 6 columns. Here are explanations of the rows:

Graduated: Whether the student graduated. This dataset only provides students that have a “Y” in the column.
GraduationTimeID: Provides the yearmonthday of the PersonID graduation.
OPEID: ID of the institution which has been converted to an 8 long string padded with “0” on the left.
InstitutionName: Name of the institution from which the PersonID graduated.
DegreeTitle: The Degree Title the PersonID graduated with. This column is a shitshow - some have values of BA, while others have it written out - Bachelor of Arts. I will need to fix this.
Major - Major the PersonID graduated with.
OPEID.6 - this is the OPEID with a string length of 6 so that it matches up with our IPEDS dataset.

The main characteristics from this dataset that I want to add to the master dataset/model are the following;

Confirmation that they graduated from a post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their first post secondary institution
The year they graduated from their last post-seconary institution
The sector of the institution(s) from which they graduated
The highest level of degree obtained by the PersonID
The degrees earned
Whether the institution(s) from which they graduated are in the same RUCA category, EDR, planning region, and state as their high school

Okay, lets first create a dataset with a unique PersonID and a column confirming that they graduated from a post secondary institution. However, we don’t want to include any students that never had a chance to complete their post-secondary institution. For example, if an individual has graduated by 2023 (the last year of the data), but is attending, then they shouldn’t be counted against the region for not having that person not “graduated”.
Essentially, what we want to identify is that in 2023, has the individual;

Graduated from a post-secondary institution,
Is still attending post-secondary institution,
Not attending post-secondary and never graduated from one.

To do this, I will need to import the NSC enrollment data, filter to 2023, and double check to see if anyone in our graduate list was attending post-secondary that year. Then ps.grad can be categorized as the following;

ps.grad: graduated from a post-secondary institution by 2023
ps.attending: attending post-secondary as of 2023
not.ps.grad: never graduated from a post-secondary institution and wasn’t enrolled in one as of 2023.



ps.enrollment <- read_csv("~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/NSCEnrollment/NSC_Enrollments.csv") %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID),
         OPEID = str_pad(OPEID, width = 8, side = "left", pad = "0"),
         OPEID.6 = str_sub(OPEID, 1, 6)) %>%
  drop_na(PersonID) %>%
  drop_na(OPEID) %>%
  filter(!EnrollmentStatus %in% c("A", "W", "D")) %>%
  mutate(enrollment.year = str_sub(EnrollmentEndTimeID, 1,4),
         enrollment.year = as.integer(enrollment.year)) %>%
  filter(enrollment.year == 2023) %>%
  select(PersonID, enrollment.year) %>%
  mutate(ps.attending.2023 = "Yes") %>%
  select(-enrollment.year) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE)

8 - Private not-for-profit, less-than 2-year

9 - Private for-profit, less-than 2-year

10 - Multiple sectors
99 - Sector unknown (not active)

Summary of students graduated from post secondary institution
We will being by summarizing the number of students in the master dataset that have graduated from a post-secondary institution. We will first look at the percentage from the total dataset and then break it up by RUCA category and regions to see if there are any significant differences.
The table below shows that the number of individuals that graduated from a post-secondary institution by 2023 was 38% while 12% were still attending a post-secondary institution.

There are 374,256 observations in the dataset. Each observation is an ACT test taken by a student in Northeast Minnesota. The unique feature here is the time it was taken. This means that a student could have taken the ACT twice and their PersonID would show up as two observations.
Out of the scores provided, I’m just going to use the composite score. Since an individual may have taken the test multiple times I will only use the highest composite score for each individual. This is how colleges do it as well.


act.highest.comp <- act.original %>%
  select(PersonID, ACTCompositeScore) %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(ACTCompositeScore == max(ACTCompositeScore)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE)

There are many paths in which an individual can take after graduating high school. What we are most concerned with is whether an individual has “meaningful” employment, when and where this employment takes place, and are there any variables that are associated with each of these pathways.
The paths that we want to identify are the following;

Meaningful employment

Meaningful employment - same county as high school

Not meaningful employment or no MN Employment record - attending post-secondary
Not meaningful employment - not attending post-secondary

We are going to assess each PersonID on which of those pathways they are at the time of their high school graduation, and each subsequent year up to 2023.

The dataset has 261,049 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.

Q: Three-quarter time

L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence

D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). Graduates not reaching the meaningful employment threshold in Minnesota hovers around 20% after the first year of graduating high school.

title: Employment
text:
Filter for “meaningful” employment
The biggest issue is how do we get a meaningful indicator on whether they were employed in the region and whether they are employed in an industry that matches their CTE experience that wasn’t just a “summer job”. We need to filter out summer jobs between college years, as well as adapt to different paths that students take.
We will define “meaningful employment” as an employment experience in which an individual works for one particular employer for 1,000 hours worked in any given year.
However, this isn’t going to just be checking to see if an individual has worked at an employer for 1,000 hours at graduation year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12. Rather, it’s going to be checking on whether they are working at an employer at grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7 and grad year +12 for which they worked 1,000 hours for an given year.
For example, a person may be employed with an employer for a few years working full-time, but part-way through grad year +7, they decide to move on. I want to make sure we capture that that individual was employed in meaningful employment even though it wasn’t full-time that particular year.
The same can go the other way. Perhaps an individual just starts employment at grad year +7 but does work full-time with that particular employer form multiple years. We will want to count that as well.
In addition, I want to capture if someone is working at an employer but isn’t quite “meaningful” but turns into meaningful later on. We will count that as well.
This will be a couple step process.

First, we will filter out the employment.original data so that only meaningful employment for each PersonID is included along with the years worked at EmploymentOrganizationID.
Collect EmploymentOrganizationID for all the years that each PersonID worked meaningful employment.
Create a new datalist of each PersonID in the master datalist with grad year, grad year +2, and +7.
Then, we will cross reference the grad year list with employment year to see if meaningful employment matches.

We will end with the following columns and labels;

PersonID has had meaningful employment since graduating high school (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - Has no MN emp record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but never
Meaningful emp - Has MN emp record and is meaningful
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023.




meaningful.employer <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, CalendarYear) %>%
  summarize(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked = sum(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked > 999) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID) %>%
  right_join(mn.emp.record[,c(1)], by = "PersonID")

title: Employment
section: Match meaningful employment and high school locations/regions.
text:
Match meaningful employment and high school locations/regions.
Now, we want to determine if the locations of meaningful employment match the counties and regions from which they graduated high school. To do this, we will import the latest master dataset so we can compare their high school locations with meaningful employment locations.
Here are the columns and labels that I need;

PersonID has had meaningful employment within the county/region (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record but not meaningful
No location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, but no match with region
Location match - Has MN emp record, had meaningful employment, and had meaningful employment in county/region
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023




emp.original.locations <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4)),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1, by = c("CountyName" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(EconomicDevelopmentRegionName = edr) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, EconomicDevelopmentRegionName, CountyName, project.pr) %>%
  rename(employment.county = CountyName,
         emp.edr = EconomicDevelopmentRegionName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = str_replace(emp.edr, "  ", " "),
         emp.edr = as.factor(emp.edr),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, " County", ""),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         employment.county = str_replace(employment.county, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         employment.county = as.factor(employment.county)) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions[,c(2,4)], by = c("employment.county" = "Name")) %>%
  rename(emp.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc) 

meaningful.emp.locations <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  left_join(emp.original.locations, by = c("PersonID", "year" = "CalendarYear", "EmploymentOrganizationID")) %>%
  mutate(emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.edr)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Hennepin", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Ramsey", "EDR 11 - 7 County Twin Cities", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "St. Louis", "EDR 3 - Arrowhead", emp.edr),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", emp.edr),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "Unknown", "Unknown", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.Dem_Desc = ifelse(employment.county == "NULL", "NULL", as.character(emp.Dem_Desc)),
         emp.edr = ifelse(employment.county == "Mahnomen", "EDR 2 - Headwaters", emp.edr))

grad.locations <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, Dem_Desc, edr, planning.region) %>%
  rename(hs.county.name = county.name,
         hs.Dem_Desc = Dem_Desc,
         hs.edr = edr,
         hs.planning.region = planning.region)

grad.emp.location.match <- grad.locations %>%
  right_join(meaningful.emp.locations, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(county.match = ifelse(employment.county == hs.county.name, 1,
                               ifelse(employment.county %in%  c("Unknown", "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)"), 0, -1)),
         edr.match = ifelse(emp.edr == hs.edr, 1,
                            ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),
         region.match = ifelse(emp.pr %in% c("Northeast"), 1,
                               ifelse(emp.edr == "Unknown", 0, -1)),
         state.match = 1) %>% 
  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(county.match = max(county.match),
         edr.match = max(edr.match),
         region.match = max(region.match),
         state.match = max(state.match)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  gather(key = "region.match", value = "confirm", 3:6) %>%
  mutate(confirm = ifelse(confirm == -1, "No location match",
                          ifelse(confirm == 0, "Unknown", "Location match")),
         grad.years.region.emp.match = paste(grad.years, ".", region.match, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years.region.emp.match, confirm) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = grad.years.region.emp.match, values_from = confirm, values_fill = "No meaningful employment") %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year.county.match, hs.grad.year.2.county.match, hs.grad.year.7.county.match, hs.grad.year.edr.match, hs.grad.year.2.edr.match, hs.grad.year.7.edr.match, hs.grad.year.region.match, hs.grad.year.2.region.match, hs.grad.year.7.region.match, hs.grad.year.state.match, hs.grad.year.2.state.match, hs.grad.year.7.state.match)

section: Match employment industry with career cluster
text:
Match employment industry with career cluster
Next we need to find a way to compare the CTE careerclusters with the actual industry from which they work. We are not able to compare majors which is a bummer. But, the careerclusters from CTE coursework does align somewhat with NAICS codes. Here’s what it looks like;

careercluster.naics.cw <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/Employment/career-cluster-naics.xlsx') %>%
  rename(cw.CareerCluster = `Career cluster code`,
         cw.CareerClusterName = `Career Cluster`,
         cw.emp.ind.code = 3,
         cw.emp.ind.name = 4)


datatable(careercluster.naics.cw, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:3)))) 






There is one industry in which two career clusters will have to be marged - Human Services and Health Science & Health Occupations. Due to this, we will create a new column with an “updated” careercluster code that includes the merged cluster.
Here are the columns and labels that I will use;

PersonID has had meaningful employment in industry from a CTE course taken (Grad year, grad year +2, grad year +7)

No MN emp record - has no MN employment record
No meaningful emp - Has MN emp record nut not meaningful
No ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, but industry does not match CTE course taken
Ind match - Has MN emp record, was meaningful, and industry and cTE course match.
After 2023 - the grad year +X is after 2023


Step 1 is to determine the industry codes for each PersonID that experienced meaningful employment for each of their “grad years”.


emp.original.for.cw <- employment.original %>%
  mutate(CalendarYear = as.integer(str_sub(TimeID, 1, 4))) %>%
  select(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, GroupCode) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, CalendarYear, EmploymentOrganizationID, GroupCode) 

cc.cw.meaningful.emp <- meaningful.emp.grad.years %>%
  left_join(emp.original.for.cw, by = c("PersonID", "EmploymentOrganizationID", "year" = "CalendarYear")) %>%
  mutate(ind.code = ifelse(GroupCode == "6215", "6215", str_sub(GroupCode, 1, 2)),
         ind.code = as.integer(ind.code)) %>%
  left_join(careercluster.naics.cw, by = c("ind.code" = "cw.emp.ind.code"))

The dataset above provides each of the meaningful employment instances during the grad years for each PersonID in the master dataset along with the GroupCode and matching CTE careercluster crosswalk for each of those employment instances. There are 50,946 rows/instances with 10 columns.
Step 2 is to merge each PersonID’s cte courses taken. with the meaningful employment dataset so we can compare if the CTE courses match the industries.


grad.cc <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-10.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, 22:46) %>%
  gather(key = "cte", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%
  filter(n.courses > 0) %>%
  rename(cte.cw = cte) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.cw, n.courses)

grad.cc.cw.naics <- cc.cw.meaningful.emp %>%
  left_join(grad.cc, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(n.courses), -1,
                               ifelse(cw.CareerCluster == cte.cw, 1, 0)),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(ind.code == 54, 1, cc.ind.match)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  summarize(max.match = max(cc.ind.match)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(cc.ind.match = ifelse(max.match == -1, "No CTE",
                               ifelse(max.match == 0, "No ind match", "Ind match")),
         cc.ind.match = ifelse(is.na(cc.ind.match), "No crosswalk", cc.ind.match)) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.years, cc.ind.match) %>%
  complete(PersonID, grad.years) %>%
  mutate(label = paste("ind.match.", grad.years, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, label, cc.ind.match) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = label, values_from = cc.ind.match)

title: Employment
section: High school grad and employment instance match
text:
High school grad and employment instance match
First, let’s look what percentage of individuals had an employment instance where the employer was located in the same county as their high school.
The table below shows that 17% of the individuals in the master dataset had meaningful employment in the same county as their high school the year they graduated. It increased to 25% two years after graduation and then 29% seven years after graduation. These percentages are after filtering out all of the “After 2023” category.


match.region.summary.total.county <- master.11 %>%
  select(PersonID, hs.grad.year.county.match, hs.grad.year.2.county.match, hs.grad.year.7.county.match) %>%
  gather(key = "hs.grad.year", value = "county.match", 2:4) %>%
  filter(county.match != "After 2023") %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year, county.match) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(hs.grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n()),
         hs.grad.year = str_sub(hs.grad.year, 1, 14),
         hs.grad.year = str_replace(hs.grad.year, "hs.grad.year.c", "hs.grad.year"))

match.region.summary.total.county.plot <- ggplot(match.region.summary.total.county, aes(hs.grad.year, pct, fill = county.match, group = county.match)) +
  geom_col_interactive(position = "dodge", aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(hs.grad.year, "\nEmployment match high school county? - ", county.match, sep = ""))) +
  geom_label(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, color = "white", size = 5, position = position_dodge(width = .9)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of individuals with meaningful employment in high school\ncounty")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  theme_bar+
  scale_fill_manual(values = brewer.pal(n = 6, "RdYlBu"),
                    guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 18))


girafe(ggobj = match.region.summary.total.county.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 10) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                 opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))      






Next, let’s check the differences by RUCA category.
Crosstabs indicate a relationship.

hs.grad.year: The more rural the high school, the slightly lower percentage of graduates have meaningful employment in the same county.
hs.grad.year.2: The same as above, but the gap is getting larger: urban/town/rural mix graduates had 27% with meaningful employment in the same county compared to just 20% for entirely rural schools.
hs.grad.year.7: The gap continues to grow: urban/town/rural mix schools had 32% with meaningful employment in their county compared to 19% in for entirely rural.

I could only use individuals who scored 3 or higher.

The dataset has 3,010,265 rows and 6 columns. Here are the columns and their definitions.

EnrollmentBeginTimeID: Begin date for the student’s period of attendance.
EnrollmentEndTimeID: End date for the student’s period of attendance.
OPEID: Office of Postsecondary Education (OPE)/FICE code of the college that the student attended (Foreign Key to IPEDSCharacteristics).
InstitutionName: Name of institution
EnrollmentStatus: The last enrollment status reported for the student. This field will have ‘N/A’ or “NULL” if the reporting college has not defined the student’s enrollment status as directory information. Here are the code definitions;

F: Full-time
Q: Three-quarter time
H: Half-time
L: Less than half-time
A: Leave of absence
W: Withdrawn
D: Deceased


Essentially, this dataset provides semester-based information - each observation is a semester/single period with the institutional information and beginning and end time of that single period (usually a semester). For example, if an individual attended South Dakota State University, attended in a “typical” fashion (fall and spring semesters), and graduated in 4 years, there would be 8 observations for that PersonID - one observation per semester.
There are a few pieces of information that I want to consolidate from this dataset;

Did the PersonID in the master dataset attend a college - yes or no?
Did the PersonID attend college during high school (PSEO), immediately after graduation or wait?
Did the PersonID attend multiple colleges - yes or no?
What type of college did the PersonID attend first?
Did the PersonID attend a public, private not-for-profit, or private or, for-profit college(s)?
At any point during their college career, did the PersonID attend a college(s) inside or outside of the Northeast Region or outside the County of their high school?

I was going to include the length of time that a PersonID attended college, but due to differences in how institutions report enrollment periods, it didn’t seem like it would be a great indicator.
The pieces of information missing in the original dataset is location and type of institution attended.To do this we will need to join the original dataset with an IPEDS dataset using opeid.
The IPEDS data and the NSC data will only match using the first 6 digits of the IPEDS OPEID values. So I will change that in the NSC data. Then I can join.


ipeds.original <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/IPEDS/IPEDS.csv') 

ipeds.sector <- ipeds.original %>%
  filter(!is.na(OPEID)) %>%
  mutate(OPEID = str_pad(OPEID, width = 8, side = "left", pad = "0"),
         OPEID.6 = str_sub(OPEID, 1, 6)) %>%
  select(Unitid, OPEID.6, City, State, FIPS, GeographicRegion, CountyCode, InstitutionSector, InstitutionName)  %>%
  mutate(CountyCode = str_pad(CountyCode, width = 5, side = "left", pad = "0"))

nsc.enrollment.ipeds<- nsc.enrollment.original %>%
  left_join(ipeds.sector, by = "OPEID.6") %>%
  drop_na(Unitid) %>%
  mutate(EnrollmentStatus = as_factor(EnrollmentStatus))

Next we will determine whether they attended a post-secondary institution inside or outside of the planning region, outside their EDR, or outside of Minnesota. Since many of the PersonID in the dataset have attended multiple institutions, we will categorize it in the following way in order to capture the combinations of attendance;

Attended inside region only (planning region, RUCA, State)
Attended inside and outside region (planning region, RUCA, state)
Attended outside region only (planning region, RUCA, state)

In order to do this we will need to combine our planning region joining documents with the nsc.enrollment.ipeds dataset. We will also need to join the master dataset with it to determine the location of the PersonID’s high school graduation location. Lastly, we will need to join up the RUCA categories for counties outside of Minnesota. Then we can start the categorization process.


dem.desc.county <- read_csv("Data/Join docs/Master-ruca-county.csv")

  select(PersonID, edr, Dem_Desc, planning.region) %>%

nsc.enrollment.location.join <- nsc.enrollment.ipeds %>%
  select(PersonID, InstitutionName, CountyCode) %>%
  left_join(dem.desc.county, by = c("CountyCode" = "State-County FIPS Code")) %>%

  rename(ps.Dem_Desc = 4,
         ps.countyfp = 8,
         ps.statefp = 9,
         ps.edr = 10,

This joined dataset gives us 245,972 rows and 11 columns. The columns beginning with “ps” are the ruca category and regions of the post-secondary institution attended. The columns beginning with “grad” are the ruca category and regions of the high school from which the PersonID graduated.
One thing that’s important is to realize that joining the nsc.enrollment dataset with the Northeast graduates dataset means we will have some NAs. Some of the students listed in the nsc.enrollment dataset aren’t in the Northeast graduates dataset since they may have graduated before 2008 or didn’t actually meet the criteria in the Northeast graduates dataset. Therefore, as we move forward, I will need to make sure to remove those NAs.
From here we can start creating new columns beginning with the RUCA category. To create this column we will gather each PersonID to examine whether or not they attended a post-secondary institution in the same RUCA category, or if they attended multiple post-secondary institutions with one institution in the same category and another not the same.


nsc.enrollment.same.ruca <- nsc.enrollment.location.join %>% 
  mutate(ps.in.same.ruca = ifelse(ps.Dem_Desc == grad.ruca, "In same RUCA", "Outside RUCA")) %>%
  select(PersonID, ps.Dem_Desc, grad.ruca, ps.in.same.ruca) %>%
  select(PersonID, ps.in.same.ruca) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, ps.in.same.ruca) %>%
  mutate(code = ifelse(ps.in.same.ruca == "In same RUCA", 1, 2)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(code = sum(code)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ps.in.same.ruca = ifelse(code == 1, "In same RUCA",
                                  ifelse(code == 2, "Outside RUCA", "Inside and outside same RUCA"))) %>%
  select(PersonID, ps.in.same.ruca)

master <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-8.csv") %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.numeric(PersonID)) 

master.9 <- master %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.confirm, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(attended.ps = ifelse(is.na(attended.ps), "No", attended.ps)) %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.first.attend, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(attended.ps.first.year = as.integer(str_sub(first.attend.ps, 1, 4)),
         attended.ps.years.hsgrad = attended.ps.first.year - grad.year,
         attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad = ifelse(attended.ps.years.hsgrad < 2, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.n.institutions, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.first.institution, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.institution.types, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.same.ruca, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.same.edr, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.same.pr, by = "PersonID") %>%
  left_join(nsc.enrollment.in.MN, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(n.institutions = ifelse(is.na(n.institutions), 0, n.institutions),
         attended.ps.years.hsgrad = ifelse(attended.ps.years.hsgrad == -14, -1, attended.ps.years.hsgrad))
