As expected, we have the same number of rows as the original master dataset - 49,816 rows. Here are the explanations of all the new columns added to the master dataset.

attended.ps - this is a confirmation that the PersonID attended a post-secondary institution at some point after graduating high school.
attended.ps.years.hsgrad - the number of years after graduation that a PersonID attended a post-secondary education. In some cases, the value is negative indicating that the PersonID attended a post-secondary institution before graduating high school.
attended.ps.within.first.year.hsgrad - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary education institution within 1 year or less from graduating high school.
n.institutions - how many post-secondary institutions the PersonID attended
first.InstitutionSector - the sector of the first post-secondary institution attended.
InstitutionSector - The sector of the post-secondary institution attended (could be multiple)
ps.in.same.ruca - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same RUCA category as their high school
ps.in.same.edr - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same economic development region as high school
ps.in.same.pr - did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in the same planning region as high school
ps.in.MN = did the PersonID attend a post-secondary institution in Minnesota.




Summary of students attending post-secondary
Lets summarize the percentage of students that attended a post-secondary institution and compare across RUCA categories.
Below is the percentage of students that attended a post-secondary institution from the entire dataset. 68% of the PersonIDs in the dataset attended a post-secondary institution at some point between 2008 and 2024.


attending.ps.pct.total <- master.9 %>%
  group_by(attended.ps) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) 

datatable(attending.ps.pct.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1:2)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3)






Now lets check to see if this percentage is statistically significantly different by RUCA group.
The cross tabs do indicate that there is a statistically significant difference in the percentage of graduates that attend a post-secondary institution by high school RUCA category. However, the percentages aren’t that different. The biggest difference is that graduates from a town/rural mix district attend at a lower rate - 65.5% compared to 672% for entirely rural districts and 68.7% from urban/town/rural mix districts.

We have 5,744,192 rows and 5 columns in this dataset. Here are the descriptions for each of the columns.

K12AsstTimeID: Day, month, and year the assessment took place.
TestName: Name of the test taken. There are 12 different tests in the dataset -

ACCESS: English proficiency,
ALTACCESS: English proficiency for special education or meet requirements
MCA-II & MCA-III: Minnesota Comprehsensive Assessments (series 2 and 3)
MOD-II, MOD-III: Modified Comprehensive Assessment, used only until 2014
MTAS & MTAS-III: Minnesota Test of Academic Skills
MTELL: an alternate assessment for students learning English (like the MTAS or MOD). MTELL was only administered from 2007-2010 during the series-II of MCAs.
SOLOM: Minnesota Student Oral Language Observation Matrix
TEAE: one of two assessments that Minnesota used to meet the requirements to test ELs in all four domains of language (the other was SOLOM). TEAE was used 2002 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012. SOLOM was used 2004 until we changed to ACCESS in 2012.

Subject: Classifies each test that is given to a student based on the areas measured. There are 8 factors;

A: Aural (listening) - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
C: Composite - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
L: Listening/Speaking
M: Math
O: Oral - ACCESS & ALTACCESS only
R: Reading
S: Science
W: Writing

GradeTested: Grade student was enrolled in when performing assessment.
AchievementLevel: Used to count the number of students in each achievement level by group such as race, gender, and ethnicity. It must be calculated from other students at a similar graden and subject for a specific year.

ACCESS students are graded on a language proficiency scale of 1 through 6.
ALT-ACCESS students are graded using a P1 through P3 and A1 through A3 scale.
There are 4 different levels for the MCA test

D: Does not meet standards
E: Exceeds standards
M: Meets Standards
P: Partially meets standards

SOLOM tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest
TEAE tests are 1-5 scale with 5 being the highest.


There are two ways in which we are going to code our graduates.
The first is to identify whether a student has been identified as an English learner. This means filtering students that have taken the ACCESS, ALT-ACCESS, MTELL, MTAS, TEAE, MOD-II, MOD-III, or SOLOM at least once in their career.
The second is be determining their highest achievement level in each subject of the MCA tests within the dataset. The dataset provides each instance of a test for each student so many are students are listed numerous times - once for each time they took a test.
Lets do this in two separate files and then join each with the master file.
Starting with identifying the EL students.


el <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(!TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(english.learner = 1)

This dataset identified 34,995 individuals who were identified as an english learner at least one time in the original dataset.
Now we will determine the highest achievement level for each subject for each student.


mca <- assessments.original %>%
  filter(TestName %in% c("MCA-II", "MCA-III")) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevel != "NULL") %>%
  droplevels() %>%
  mutate(AchievementLevelCode = ifelse(AchievementLevel == "D", 1,
                                       ifelse(AchievementLevel == "P", 2,
                                              ifelse(AchievementLevel == "M", 3, 4))))

mca.highest <- mca %>%
  group_by(PersonID, Subject) %>%
  filter(AchievementLevelCode == max(AchievementLevelCode)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, Subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(mca.subject = paste("MCA.", Subject, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, mca.subject, AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  mutate(id = seq(n())) %>%
  spread(key = mca.subject, value = AchievementLevelCode) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  fill(MCA.M, .direction = c("downup")) %>%
  fill(MCA.R, .direction = "downup") %>%
  fill(MCA.S, .direction = "downup") %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-id)

text:
The next dataset is individuals that were enrolled in CTE courses. I’m first going to load the entire dataset, then clean it up, and then I will merge it with my master/NE graduate dataset.


cte.enrollment.original <- read_csv('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/CTEEnrollment.csv') %>%
  mutate(PersonID = as.integer(PersonID)) %>%
  filter(FiscalYearTimeID != "NULL") %>%
  mutate(CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "26" & CareerClusterName == "Diversified Youth Apprenticeship", "25", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = ifelse(CareerCluster == "NULL", "0", CareerCluster),
         CareerCluster = str_replace(CareerCluster, "Design", "11"),
         CareerCluster = as.integer(CareerCluster))


career.cluster.codes.names.original <- read_xlsx('/Users/kellyasche/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-kasche@ruralmn.org/My Drive/Research/FY25-27/FY26/OHE Journey to meaningful employment/Data/SLEDS/CTEEnrollment/career-cluster-codes-names_from SLEDS_March2025.xlsx') %>%
  mutate(cte.year = ifelse(Introduced > 2020, 2021, Discontinued),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(Introduced) & is.na(Discontinued), 2021, cte.year),
         cte.year = ifelse(is.na(cte.year), 2020, cte.year),
         CareerClusterName.new = as_factor(CareerClusterName.new))


career.cluster.codes.names.addendum <- data.frame(`CareerCluster` = c(0, 1, 2),
                                                  CareerClusterName.new = c("NULL", "Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources", "Architecture & Construction"),
                                                  Status = c("Retired", "Retired", "Retired"),
                                                  Introduced = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  Discontinued = c(2021, 2021, 2021),
                                                  cte.year = c(2020, 2020, 2020))

career.cluster.codes.names <- career.cluster.codes.names.original %>%
  rbind(career.cluster.codes.names.addendum)

cte.enrollment.master <- cte.enrollment.original %>%
  mutate(year = str_sub(FiscalYearTimeID, 1, 4),
         year = as.integer(year),

  left_join(career.cluster.codes.names[,c(1,2,6)], by = c("CareerCluster", "cte.year")) %>%
  select(-CareerClusterName, -year, -cte.year) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerClusterName.new)

There seems to be a minor coding error in the careercluster column. For one particular class, it was consistently labeled “Information Technology” even though the field requires a number value. In addition, “information Technology” doesn’t seem to match the course due to the following information;

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student
text:
Summary - Number of CTE courses taken by a student

We’ll start with summarising the number of cte courses the observations have taken.
The tables below show that the average number of CTE courses taken by all PersonID in the master dataset is 2.29 with a standard deviation of +/-2.39. This is a high standard deviation meaning there are values quite far from the mean.
The second row of the table shows the average number of CTE courses taken by individuals who took at least one CTE course. The average jumps up a bit to 3.20 with a standard deviation of 2.25.


cte.n.courses.summary.total <- master.4 %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "All graduates",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))

cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents <- master.4 %>%
  filter(total.cte.courses.taken > 0) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(total.cte.courses.taken),
            median = median(total.cte.courses.taken),
            sd = sd(total.cte.courses.taken),
            n = comma(n(), accuracy = 1),
            min = min(total.cte.courses.taken),
            max = max(total.cte.courses.taken)) %>%
  mutate(population = "Only graduates with CTE courses > 0",
         mean = comma(mean, accuracy = .01),
         sd = comma(sd, accuracy = .01))
  
cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents <- cte.n.courses.summary.total %>%
  rbind(cte.n.courses.summary.ctestudents) %>%
  select(population, n, mean, median, sd, min, max)

datatable(cte.n.courses.summary.total.ctestudents, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top")






Below is a chart showing the distribution of CTE courses taken by individuals. This shows that a a large majority of students take 5 courses or less.


master.4.hist <- master.4 %>%
  mutate(key = seq(n())) %>%
  select(key, total.cte.courses.taken)

cte.n.courses.taken.dist.plot <- ggplot(master.4.hist, aes(total.cte.courses.taken)) +
  geom_histogram_interactive(aes(data_id = key, tooltip = paste("N = ", comma(..count.., accuracy = 1), "\nPercent: ", percent(..count.. / sum(..count..), accuracy = .1)))) +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Histogram - N CTE courses")+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::comma)+
  theme_line+
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 16))

  girafe(ggobj = cte.n.courses.taken.dist.plot, width_svg = 10) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))






The following table shows that nearly three-quarters of the students took at least one CTE course.


cte.pct <- master.4 %>%
  mutate(took.CTE = ifelse(total.cte.courses.taken > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  group_by(took.CTE) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup()  %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

datatable(cte.pct, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(columnDefs = list(list(className = "dt-center", targets = 1)))) %>%
  formatCurrency(2, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(3, digits = 1)






Up next is to see if the percentage of students taking a CTE course varies significantly by RUCA group.
There is a significant difference in whether a student has taken at least one CTE course and their high school county RUCA category. Although 72% of all graduates took at least one CTE course, that percentage is highest in more rural districts. 85.7% took at least one CTE course in entirely rural districts while 80.2% took at least one in town/rural mix districts. 67.5% took at least one in our urban/town/rural mix districts.
Of those students that took at least 1 CTE course, the average number of CTE courses taken ranged from 3.7 in our entirely rural districts to 3.1 in urban/town/rural mix districts.

title: CTEEnrollment
section: Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
text:
Summary - CareerCluster of CTE courses taken
Let’s dig into the breadth of CTE course concentrations a graduate would take by looking at the proportion of graduates that took at least one course within a concentration.
The table below shows that nearly a third of all graduates took a CTE course in Transportation, Distribution & Logistics, followed by 20% in Manufacturing, and 16% in each Architecture & Construction and Human Services.


cte.cf.prop <- master.4 %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  mutate(cte.cf.taken = ifelse(n.courses > 0, "Yes", "No")) %>%
  tabyl(CareerCluster, cte.cf.taken) %>%
  mutate(pct.taken.cf = Yes / (Yes + No)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(pct.taken.cf))

datatable(cte.cf.prop, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE,
          options = list(scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
  formatCurrency(2:3, "", digits = 0) %>%
  formatPercentage(4)






Now we will take a look at the breakdown of the number of times a CTE courses has been taken within a CareerCluster for each PersonID. I expect there to be a lot of variation in this data since different schools might focus on different types of CTE offerings depending on the local employment makeup.
First, lets look at the concentrations of courses taken across CareerClusters.
Not surprisingly, Transportation, Distribution & Logistics was the careercluster with the highest percentage of courses taken with 19.6%. This was followed by manufacturing with 12.4% and architecture and construction with 11.0% of CTE courses taken in that CareerCluster.


cte.cf.concentration.total <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", 2:ncol(.)) %>%
  group_by(CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = .1)) %>%
  arrange(CareerCluster)

  datatable(cte.cf.concentration.total, class = "cell-border stripe", filter = "top", rownames = FALSE)






Lets see how this looks broken down by county.
The county maps do show some differences in percentages across career clusters. Manufacturing was consistently offered and taken across the region, as well as transportation, distribution and logistics and Human Services.
Koochiching has a high percentage of students that take health science & health occupations as well as human services.


cte.cf.concentration.county <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, county.name, countyfp,  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses",  `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(county.name, countyfp) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) %>%
  left_join(mn_counties[,c(5,7)], by = "countyfp")

cte.cf.concentration.county.map <- ggplot(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.county, pct > .05)) +
  facet_wrap(~CareerClusterName, ncol = 2,
             labeller = label_wrap_gen(15)) +
  geom_sf_interactive(color = "grey85", aes(geometry = geometry, fill = pct, data_id = countyfp, tooltip = paste(county.name, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of courses taken in this CareerCluster: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  theme_sf+
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "PuBu", direction = 1, labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = str_wrap("Percent of CTE courses taken within each CareerCluster by county", 39)) +
  theme(legend.box.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0),
        text = element_text(size = 16),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.county.map, height_svg = 20) %>%
  girafe_options(opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))






The next big question is whether these percentages vary by year. Are there any trends?
This is honestly a bit surprising. The chart raises a couple of questions.
There was a big increase in the transportation, distribution and logistics career cluster in the mid-2010s but has declined substantially since that time. Health science and health occupations has been growing steadily as well as architecture and construction.


cte.cf.concentration.year <- master.4 %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  gather(key = "CareerCluster", value = "n.courses", `ACTE-SPED`:`Youth Apprenticeship`) %>%
  group_by(grad.year, CareerCluster) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n.courses)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(grad.year > 2006) %>%
  mutate(data_id = seq(n())) %>%
  rename(CareerClusterName = CareerCluster) 


cte.cf.concentration.year.plot <- ggplot(cte.cf.concentration.year, aes(grad.year, pct, color = CareerClusterName)) +
  geom_point_interactive(size = 3, aes(data_id = data_id, tooltip = paste(CareerClusterName, "\nYear: ", grad.year, "\nCareerCluster: ", CareerClusterName, "\nPercent of CTE courses taken: ", percent(pct, accuracy = .1), sep = ""))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x="", y = "", color="", title = "Percent of taken CTE courses")+
  geom_label(data = filter(cte.cf.concentration.year, grad.year == max(cte.cf.concentration.year$grad.year)), aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = .1)), show.legend = FALSE, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::percent)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2050, 2),
                     guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) +
  theme_line+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = guide_legend(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        text = element_text(size = 14))

  girafe(ggobj = cte.cf.concentration.year.plot, width_svg = 10, height_svg = 7) %>%
    girafe_options(opts_selection(type = "none"),
                   opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
                   opts_sizing(rescale = FALSE))







write_csv(master.4, "Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-4.csv")

The dataset employment.disconnected.grad.year.5 provides the following;

PersonID: Identifies the graduate from Northeast Minnesota
TimeID: Last day of fiscal quarter
EmploymentOrganizationID: An internal identification for each employer.
EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked: The total number of hours worked by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeQuarterlyWages: The total wages earned by an employee at an employer’s location during a specific calendar quarter
EmployeeTenure: The total number of quarters a worker has been employeed by an organization at a specific location, up to an including the current calendar quarter
IndustryID: Auto generated ID code for a record in the Industry dimension.
USIndustryCode: Six-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
GroupCode: Four-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) code
OwnershipCode: A classification system based upon the controlling interest of the establishment primarily designed to distinguish between governmental and non-governmental establishments

10 = Federal government
20 = State government
30 = Local government
50 = Private

EmployerLocationTotalWagesPaid: The total wages paid to all workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
QuarterlyAverageEmployment: The average number of workers employeed by an organization at a specific location during a specific calendar quarter
County: Minnesota county code to which this institution belongs. This can be used as a foreign key into the Geography dimension on MNCounty.

Link to codes

CountyName: The name of the county corresponding to the County and MNCounty Codes for this Location.
MNCounty: County Code for this location as assigned by the state of Minnesota.

Link to codes City: All of the city data is NA

Okay, we now have a dataset that contains every individual that was categorized as “Not meaningufl, not attening ps” 5-years after completing high school along with each employment instance that had during the year that matches 5 years after high school. Now we can start to determine if their not meaningful workforce participation took place inside or outside the region, or both. To do this, we will join employment.disconnected.hs.grad.year.5 with my county.regions dataset so that I will be able to identify whether the employer was located in EDR 3 or not. Then I will categorize each individual into the three categories.

in.out.disconnected.grad.year.5 <- employment.disconnected.hs.grad.year.5 %>%
  select(PersonID, County, CountyName, hs.grad.year.5) %>%
  mutate(County = formatC(County, width = 3, flag = "0"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen"),
         County = ifelse(CountyName == "Mahnomen", "087", County),
         County = ifelse(CountyName == "St. Louis", "137", County),
         County = ifelse(CountyName == "Hennepin", "053", County),
         County = ifelse(CountyName == "Ramsey", "123", County),
         County = ifelse(CountyName == "Scott", "139", County)) %>%
  filter(CountyName != "Statewide (i.e. no fixed location)") %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1[,c(1, 10)], by = c("County" = "countyfp")) %>%
  filter(CountyName != "Unknown") %>%
  rename(emp.County = County,
         emp.CountyName = CountyName,
         emp.pr = project.pr) %>%
  mutate(not.meaningful.region = ifelse(emp.pr == "Northeast", -1, 1)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, not.meaningful.region) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(not.meaningful.location = ifelse(sum(not.meaningful.region) == -1, "Employed in region",
                                          ifelse(sum(not.meaningful.region) == 0, "Employed in and out of region", "Employed out of region"))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(PersonID, not.meaningful.location) %>%
  distinct(PersonID, .keep_all = TRUE)

The original dataset provides whether the student was a basic participant, basic concentrator, basic completor, and/or a centrentrator 150 when taking a CTE course. It looks like each observation is unique by grade of the student. This means that one PersonID can have multiple observations.
In order to determine how I want to organize this data so that each observation represents the full characteristics of each PersonID I need to understand how these values are defined.

Basic Participant: Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes one or more state-approved CTE course(s).
Basic Concentrator: this is the old standard for years and required the student complete 240 hours. Any student successfully enrolled in a single CTE field for more than 240 hours (successful is defined as passing grade).
Basic Completor: any concentrator who attains academic and technical knowledge and skills and graduates from high school.
Concentrator 150: This is the new standard - Any grade 9-12 student who successfully completes 150+ course hours (or more) as part of a state-approved secondary CTE program, within one career field.

Judging by these definitions, it seems that we will want three categories;

Those that participated in a CTE course but were not a concentrator or a completor, and
Those that participated in a CTE course and graduated as a concentrator.
Those that did not participate in a CTE course.

So essentially, filtering this dataset to provide the “highest level achieved” in terms of CTE coursework. We will focus on filtering this dataset to the highest level achieved and will then join with the graduate list which will have all the individuals that did not participate in any CTE courses.


graduate <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/Master-4.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID)

cte.concentrator.cat <- cte.demographics.original %>%
  gather(key = "cte.achievement", value = "yes.or.no", 4:7) %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "Null") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "NULL") %>%
  filter(yes.or.no != "N") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = as.factor(cte.achievement),
         yes.or.no = as.factor(yes.or.no),
         cte.achievement.code = ifelse(cte.achievement == "BasicParticipant", 0, 1)) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement, cte.achievement.code) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarise(cte.achievement.code = sum(cte.achievement.code)) %>%

  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(cte.achievement.code == 0, "CTE Participant", "CTE Concentrator or Completor")) %>%
  select(PersonID, cte.achievement) %>%
  right_join(graduate, by = "PersonID") %>%
  mutate(cte.achievement = ifelse(is.na(cte.achievement), "No CTE", cte.achievement))

title: Question on non-college grads and workforce categories timeline
text:
Methodology
We will do two steps; 1. Description of datasets for both the disconnect level categories and the regional disconnection categories. 2. Test the relationships between variables and these categories.
The variables we will use are; - Demographic - RaceEthnicity - SpecialEdStatus - High school characteristics - Dem_Desc - avg.unemp.rate - avg.wages.pct.state - High school academics - pseo.participant - took.ACT - cte.achievement - total.cte.courses.taken - ACTCompositeScore - MCA.M - MCA.R - MCA.S - Post-secondary - attended.ps

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Special Education Status
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between Special Education status and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3110.70, Cramer’s V = 0.258, p < .001, N = 46,777

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 829.87, Cramer’s V = 0.155, p < .001, N = 34,683

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 231.15, Cramer’s V = 0.108, p < .001, N = 19,828

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and weakens over time, but the relationship remains significant. The primary pattern is that SpecialEd students are less likely to attend postsecondary and more likely to be in not meaningful or disconnected outcomes. While regional meaningful employment is roughly equal at Year 1, by Years 5 and 10 non-SpecialEd students pull ahead in meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is nearly the same for SpecialEd (15.6%) and non-SpecialEd (15.3%). The sharpest differences are in education and disconnection: only 21.4% of SpecialEd students are attending postsecondary compared to 52.5% of non-SpecialEd, and 25.1% of SpecialEd students are disconnected compared to 9.3% of non-SpecialEd. This points to an early divergence where SpecialEd students are disproportionately outside of education and tracked employment.
5 Years After Graduation: Gaps in regional meaningful employment begin to open (SpecialEd 24.6% vs. non-SpecialEd 26.8%). SpecialEd students are still much less likely to be in postsecondary (6.8% vs. 17.6%) and more likely to be not meaningful (29.1% vs. 20.0%) or disconnected (30.0% vs. 19.5%). By this stage, non-SpecialEd students strengthen their advantage in both education and regional meaningful jobs.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment widens further (SpecialEd 24.7% vs. non-SpecialEd 29.9%). Non-SpecialEd students are also more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (20.6% vs. 11.7%). SpecialEd students remain more concentrated in disconnected outcomes (36.9% vs. 31.7%). The long-term trajectory shows that SpecialEd students are less attached to meaningful regional work and face persistent disadvantages in education and quality employment.

Strongest Associations
- Special Education Status (V = 0.258 at Year 1) and Economic Status (V = 0.238 at Year 1) emerge as the strongest predictors of post-graduation outcomes. Both show very large disparities in postsecondary participation and elevated risks of disconnection. In terms of regional meaningful employment, SpecialEd students start at parity but fall behind by Year 5 and 10, while higher economic status students consistently hold an edge.
Moderately Strong Associations
- English Learner status (V = 0.188 at Year 1) also shows a strong early effect, with EL students much less likely to enter postsecondary pathways and far more likely to be disconnected. The disadvantage persists through Year 10, with especially large gaps in meaningful regional employment and disconnection rates.
- Gender (V = 0.109 at Year 1) presents more moderate differences. Males are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while females dominate postsecondary enrollment. These gaps diminish but persist slightly by Year 10.
Weakest Associations
- Race/Ethnicity (V = 0.067 at Year 1) shows weaker overall associations but still highlights persistent inequities. White graduates are more likely to secure meaningful regional jobs, while American Indian, Black, Hispanic, and Asian/PI students show consistently lower rates of regional employment and higher disconnection. Although the effect sizes are weaker, the equity implications are substantial.
Overall Insight
Among demographic variables, SpecialEdStatus, Economic Status, and English Learner status stand out as the most influential factors shaping post-graduation outcomes, particularly through disparities in meaningful employment in the region. Gender plays a secondary but notable role, while Race/Ethnicity shows weaker statistical association but nonetheless reflects important and persistent disparities in equity and opportunity.

title: Pathways After High School – Northeast Minnesota
text:
This one-page overview integrates effect size tables, key insights, and a visual comparison chart across all four major sections of analysis.




Demographics
- Strongest predictor: SpecialEd Status (V = 0.258, Yr 1).
- Demographics fade in importance over time; SpecialEd and Race/Ethnicity remain the most relevant.
High School Characteristics
- Local economic conditions (unemployment, wages) significantly shape early outcomes (F = 53.1 for unemployment, Yr 1).
- Rural/urban divides also matter, but effects diminish by Year 10.
High School Accomplishments
- Academic/college-prep measures (ACT, MCA, PSEO, AP) → statewide pathways, less regional attachment.
- CTE achievement and course load → strongest predictors of regional meaningful employment.
- MCA Math has the largest overall predictive power (F = 1344.5, Yr 1).
Postsecondary Experiences
- The most powerful overall predictors.
- Attendance and graduation separate students into statewide vs. regional pathways.
- Credential level and location nuance outcomes: regional/2-year credentials anchor locally, 4-year/out-of-state expand mobility.







Effect Sizes Overview







Regional meaningful employment is most strongly tied to CTE in high school and regional/2-year postsecondary pathways.

Statewide employment and mobility stem from academic success and 4-year/out-of-state credentials.

Disconnection is concentrated among non-attenders, non-graduates, and those with weaker preparation, amplified by local economic stressors.

This highlights a dual pathway model:
1. Academic + 4-year trajectories → statewide mobility and higher credentials.
2. CTE + regional PS pathways → strong anchoring in the local workforce.
Both are vital in shaping Northeast Minnesota’s labor market outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Range School Context
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between attending a Range school and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 173.72, Cramer’s V = 0.061, p < .001, N = 46,777【487†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 63.68, Cramer’s V = 0.043, p < .001, N = 34,683【488†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 57.03, Cramer’s V = 0.054, p < .001, N = 19,828【489†source】

The strength of association is weak overall but consistent. The primary relationship is that Range school students are more likely to achieve meaningful employment in the region compared to non‑Range peers, though differences in postsecondary attendance and disconnection are modest.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is slightly higher among Range school students (16.6% vs. 15.0%). Range students are also somewhat more likely to be attending postsecondary (52.1% vs. 46.6%) and less likely to be in not meaningful work (17.8% vs. 21.8%). Disconnection is lower for Range students (10.2% vs. 12.1%)【487†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment advantages grow, with 29.3% of Range graduates employed in the region compared to 25.8% of non‑Range peers. Postsecondary enrollment remains somewhat higher (17.3% vs. 15.7%), while not meaningful and disconnection outcomes are slightly lower for Range graduates (19.6% vs. 21.7% and 19.3% vs. 21.5%)【488†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: The gap in regional meaningful employment becomes more pronounced: 34.0% of Range graduates vs. 28.0% of non‑Range graduates. Range graduates maintain comparable statewide meaningful employment (18.4% vs. 19.7%), and their disconnection remains modestly lower (29.7% vs. 33.1%)【489†source】. The long‑term trend indicates that Range school students are more attached to regional meaningful work than non‑Range peers.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Average County Unemployment Rate (Sophomore–Senior Years)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the county unemployment rate during high school and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA on unemployment rate across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 46772) = 12.55, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 34678) = 13.03, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 19745) = 9.69, p < .001

Effects are modest but reliable across years.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Attending postsecondary comes from higher‑unemployment counties than Meaningful employment in the region (Δ = +0.118, p < .001).
- Not meaningful and No MN record are also higher than Meaningful region (Δ ≈ +0.07 to +0.08, both p < .05).
- Takeaway: in the first year, regional meaningful employment is associated with comparatively lower local unemployment than several alternative pathways.
Year 5:
- Meaningful MN (statewide) > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.146, p < .001).
- Attending ps and No MN record are lower than Meaningful MN (Δ ≈ −0.091 and −0.088, both p ≤ .004).
- Takeaway: by five years out, statewide meaningful employment is associated with higher‑unemployment counties than regional meaningful jobs, while continued schooling and no record skew lower than statewide meaningful.
Year 10:
- Meaningful MN > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.088, p = .0009).
- Not meaningful > Meaningful region (Δ = +0.067, p = .022).
- No MN record < Meaningful MN and < Not meaningful (Δ = −0.103 and −0.082; p ≤ .002).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower unemployment contexts than statewide meaningful and not meaningful routes; those with no MN record tend to come from lower‑unemployment counties than peers in statewide/not‑meaningful outcomes.
Overall, the pattern suggests that students from lower‑unemployment counties are more likely to land in meaningful employment within the region, whereas higher‑unemployment origins are more often associated with statewide meaningful, not meaningful, or continued schooling pathways.

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
As we move from descriptive analysis to predictive modeling, the goal is to retain the strongest predictors while removing weaker or redundant ones.
Below is a structured list by section.



Keep / Prioritize
- SpecialEd Status (strongest demographic predictor)
- Race/Ethnicity (moderate strength, important equity covariate)
Drop / Deprioritize
- Gender (weak, V ≈ .05–.10, fades over time)
- English Learner (very weak, V < .07, small group sizes)
- Economic Status (moderate but weaker compared to later predictors; may retain as a control if needed)




Keep / Prioritize
- Dem_Desc (Rural/Urban) – moderate, useful contextual control
- Avg. Unemployment – strong early F-values, local context matters
- Avg. Wages % State – strong F-values, economic environment indicator
Drop / Deprioritize
- Range School (very weak effect, V ≈ .03–.05)




Keep / Prioritize
- ACT (took ACT, ACT Composite Score) – strong, differentiates pathways
- MCA (Math strongest, Reading & Science secondary) – critical academic predictors
- CTE Achievement – anchors to regional meaningful employment
- Total CTE Courses Taken – consistent predictor of regional attachment
- PSEO Participation – strong early differentiator of statewide vs regional pathways
Drop / Deprioritize
- SAT Taken (consistently weak, V ≈ .07, redundant with ACT)
- AP Exam (moderate, but less powerful than ACT/MCA; may be dropped if multicollinearity is high)




Keep / Prioritize
- Attended Postsecondary Within First Year – strongest early effect (V > .5)
- Ever Attended Postsecondary – very strong differentiator (V > .6)
- Postsecondary Graduation – critical predictor of long-term stability
- Highest Credential Level – strong differentiator between statewide vs regional pathways
- Graduation Location – strong anchor for regional vs statewide attachment
Drop / Deprioritize
- Institution Sector – moderate only (V ≈ .14–.16); may be redundant with credential level & location





Drop: Gender, English Learner, Range School, SAT Taken, possibly AP Exam, possibly Institution Sector

Keep: All others, with focus on SpecialEd, Race/Ethnicity, local economic indicators, ACT/MCA, CTE, and Postsecondary attendance/graduation/credentials.

This balances parsimony (leaner model) with coverage (keeping conceptually important drivers of outcomes).

- Economic Status (moderate but weaker compared to later predictors; may retain as a control if needed)

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
Keep / Prioritize
- Dem_Desc (Rural/Urban) – moderate, useful contextual control
- Avg. Unemployment – strong early F-values, local context matters
- Avg. Wages % State – strong F-values, economic environment indicator
Drop / Deprioritize
- Range School (very weak effect, V ≈ .03–.05)

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
Keep / Prioritize
- ACT (took ACT, ACT Composite Score) – strong, differentiates pathways
- MCA (Math strongest, Reading & Science secondary) – critical academic predictors
- CTE Achievement – anchors to regional meaningful employment
- Total CTE Courses Taken – consistent predictor of regional attachment
- PSEO Participation – strong early differentiator of statewide vs regional pathways
Drop / Deprioritize
- SAT Taken (consistently weak, V ≈ .07, redundant with ACT)
- AP Exam (moderate, but less powerful than ACT/MCA; may be dropped if multicollinearity is high)

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
Keep / Prioritize
- Attended Postsecondary Within First Year – strongest early effect (V > .5)
- Ever Attended Postsecondary – very strong differentiator (V > .6)
- Postsecondary Graduation – critical predictor of long-term stability
- Highest Credential Level – strong differentiator between statewide vs regional pathways
- Graduation Location – strong anchor for regional vs statewide attachment
Drop / Deprioritize
- Institution Sector – moderate only (V ≈ .14–.16); may be redundant with credential level & location

title: Model-Ready Variable Recommendations
text:
Drop: Gender, English Learner, Range School, SAT Taken, possibly AP Exam, possibly Institution Sector

Keep: All others, with focus on SpecialEd, Race/Ethnicity, local economic indicators, ACT/MCA, CTE, and Postsecondary attendance/graduation/credentials.

This balances parsimony (leaner model) with coverage (keeping conceptually important drivers of outcomes).

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
CTE Achievement
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between CTE achievement (Concentrator/Completer, Participant, No CTE) and post‑graduation outcomes across all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(8) = 508.14, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 46,777【663†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(8) = 307.50, Cramer’s V = 0.067, p < .001, N = 34,683【664†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 174.53, Cramer’s V = 0.066, p < .001, N = 19,828【665†source】

The associations are modest but consistent. The clearest relationship is that CTE Concentrators/Completers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region, while students with no CTE are more likely to be in postsecondary or outside regional attachment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is highest for CTE Concentrators/Completers (19.4%), compared to Participants (15.1%) and No CTE students (12.6%). Postsecondary enrollment is much higher among No CTE (51.3%) and Participants (49.2%) than Concentrators/Completers (41.5%). This suggests that CTE pathways steer students more quickly into regional work while non‑CTE students delay employment through postsecondary【663†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: The regional employment gap persists: 31.9% for Concentrators/Completers vs. 27.2% for Participants and 22.9% for No CTE. Postsecondary attendance is relatively low across all groups (13–17%), but still higher for those without CTE. Concentrators/Completers maintain stronger local employment connections, while non‑CTE students lean slightly more toward statewide employment (15.7%)【664†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains strongest among Concentrators/Completers (34.6%), compared to Participants (29.1%) and No CTE students (25.5%). Statewide meaningful employment is more evenly distributed, while disconnection is highest among those with No CTE (35.5%). The long‑term pattern confirms that CTE achievement reinforces regional employment pathways, while students outside CTE are more likely to leave the region or experience disconnection【665†source】.
Overall, CTE achievement consistently predicts stronger regional workforce attachment, distinguishing Concentrators/Completers as the group most likely to remain engaged in meaningful employment within the region over time.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Science (MCA.S)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Science scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 37501) = 544.02, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 26050) = 160.29, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 11879) = 81.74, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant through 10 years. The key pattern is that higher MCA Science scores are associated with postsecondary education and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score substantially higher than regional meaningful (+0.38, p < .001).
- Statewide meaningful (+0.07) also scores higher than regional meaningful (p = .025).
- Not meaningful (−0.07) and No MN record (−0.12) score below postsecondary.
- Takeaway: early on, regional meaningful work is tied to lower MCA-S scores, while education and statewide jobs are tied to higher scores.
Year 5:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.25) and postsecondary (+0.32) are far above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- No MN record (+0.11) is also higher.
- Not meaningful (−0.04) is slightly below regional meaningful (p = .044).
- Takeaway: by 5 years, the gap widens, with statewide and postsecondary pathways clearly tied to higher MCA-S scores, while regional meaningful remains lower.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.27) and No MN record (+0.18) score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (−0.31) scores well below regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains linked to lower MCA-S scores, while higher scores push students into statewide jobs or out of tracked MN employment.
Overall, MCA Science mirrors the MCA Reading pattern: academic achievement is strongly tied to educational and statewide pathways, while lower achievement is associated with stronger regional attachment or risk of weaker employment outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
SAT Test Participation (SAT Taken)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between taking the SAT and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 228.74, Cramer’s V = 0.070, p < .001, N = 46,777【595†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 188.76, Cramer’s V = 0.074, p < .001, N = 34,683【596†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 99.99, Cramer’s V = 0.071, p < .001, N = 19,828【597†source】

The effect sizes are small but consistent. The key pattern is that SAT takers are far more likely to attend postsecondary education, while non‑takers are more likely to enter meaningful employment in the region.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: SAT takers are overwhelmingly in postsecondary (73.5% vs. 47.3% for non‑takers). Regional meaningful employment is much lower for SAT takers (3.2% vs. 15.5%), while disconnection is also somewhat lower (9.0% vs. 11.7%)【595†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: SAT takers maintain higher postsecondary enrollment (30.1% vs. 15.8%). Regional meaningful employment is still much lower (7.6% vs. 26.8%). Interestingly, SAT takers are slightly more likely to be in meaningful employment statewide (18.2% vs. 15.1%). Disconnection is higher among SAT takers (28.6% vs. 20.9%)【596†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: SAT takers continue to show very low regional meaningful employment (11.5% vs. 29.5%), while statewide meaningful employment is similar (18.6% vs. 19.4%). Disconnection is much higher among SAT takers (55.9% vs. 32.0%)【597†source】.
Overall, SAT participation identifies a small group of students who overwhelmingly pursue postsecondary initially, but long‑term outcomes show weak regional attachment and much higher disconnection, suggesting that SAT takers may be more mobile, pursue opportunities outside the region or state, or leave tracked employment systems altogether.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Post-Secondary Enrollment Options (PSEO) Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between PSEO participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 3076.21, Cramer’s V = 0.290, p < .001, N = 36,625【542†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 430.00, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 24,531【543†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 77.28, Cramer’s V = 0.089, p < .001, N = 9,676【544†source】

The strength of association is very strong in the first year but weakens considerably over time. The primary relationship is that PSEO participants are much more likely to pursue postsecondary education, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment early on.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is higher among non‑PSEO students (18.4%) compared to PSEO participants (12.6%). In contrast, PSEO participants are far more likely to be attending postsecondary (61.8% vs. 33.6%). Disconnection is notably lower among PSEO participants (6.5% vs. 16.2%)【542†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment gaps narrow (28.1% non‑PSEO vs. 25.1% PSEO). Importantly, PSEO participants surpass non‑participants in meaningful employment statewide (18.0% vs. 13.3%). Postsecondary attendance is higher among PSEO students (19.1% vs. 11.9%), while disconnection is lower (18.7% vs. 23.5%)【543†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is relatively similar (29.7% non‑PSEO vs. 26.8% PSEO). PSEO participants maintain higher statewide meaningful employment (24.0% vs. 16.9%), while disconnection rates are similar (~32%). The long‑term pattern suggests PSEO participants transition from education into statewide meaningful jobs, while non‑participants retain an edge in regional meaningful employment【544†source】.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
MCA Reading (MCA.R)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between MCA Reading scores and post‑graduation outcomes in all three timeframes (ANOVA across outcome groups):

1 year after graduation: F(4, 42500) = 689.45, p < .001

5 years after graduation: F(4, 31013) = 119.45, p < .001

10 years after graduation: F(3, 17590) = 237.15, p < .001

The results show a very strong early effect that remains significant over time. The primary pattern is that higher MCA Reading scores are associated with postsecondary enrollment and statewide meaningful employment, while lower scores are more tied to regional meaningful employment or not meaningful/disconnected outcomes.
Interpretation Over Time (Tukey HSD highlights)
Year 1:
- Postsecondary attendees score about +0.26 higher than regional meaningful workers (p < .001).
- Not meaningful (+0.09) and No MN record (+0.14) also score higher than regional meaningful (p ≤ .02).
- Takeaway: regional meaningful employment is linked to lower reading scores, while higher scores track into postsecondary and other categories.
Year 5:
- Postsecondary (+0.21), statewide meaningful (+0.17), and No MN record (+0.08) all score above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores slightly below regional meaningful (−0.17, p < .001).
- Takeaway: by five years, regional meaningful employment sits lower on the MCA-R spectrum, while postsecondary and statewide jobs skew higher.
Year 10:
- Statewide meaningful (+0.18) and No MN record (+0.14) are significantly above regional meaningful (p < .001).
- Not meaningful scores considerably lower (−0.25, p < .001).
- Takeaway: a decade out, regional meaningful employment remains tied to lower MCA-R scores, with higher scores concentrated in statewide meaningful employment or outside tracked records.
Overall, MCA Reading reinforces that academic achievement predicts longer-term educational and statewide work pathways, while lower scores are associated with stronger regional attachment but also greater risk of not meaningful outcomes.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
AP Exam Participation
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between AP exam participation and post-graduation outcomes in all three timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(4) = 822.44, Cramer’s V = 0.133, p < .001, N = 46,777【581†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(4) = 301.32, Cramer’s V = 0.093, p < .001, N = 34,683【582†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(3) = 113.60, Cramer’s V = 0.076, p < .001, N = 19,828【583†source】

The strength of association is strongest in the first year and declines over time, though remains statistically significant. The primary relationship is that AP exam participants are much more likely to attend postsecondary, while non‑participants are more likely to enter meaningful regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
1 Year After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment is substantially higher among non‑AP students (16.1% vs. 7.7%), while AP exam participants are much more likely to be in postsecondary (68.8% vs. 45.7%). Disconnection is lower for AP participants (6.7% vs. 12.2%)【581†source】.
5 Years After Graduation: Non‑AP students retain an advantage in regional meaningful employment (27.4% vs. 17.1%), while AP participants show higher rates of statewide meaningful employment (19.8% vs. 14.7%) and continued postsecondary enrollment (23.7% vs. 15.3%). Disconnection rates are similar (~21%)【582†source】.
10 Years After Graduation: Regional meaningful employment remains higher for non‑AP students (29.9% vs. 22.7%). AP participants hold an advantage in statewide meaningful employment (27.0% vs. 18.7%). Disconnection is slightly higher for AP participants (36.0% vs. 32.1%), suggesting some trade‑off in regional attachment over time【583†source】.
Overall, AP exam participation sorts students into pathways favoring education and statewide employment, while non‑participants maintain stronger ties to regional meaningful employment.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation by Institution Sector (ps.grad.InstitutionSector)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between the sector of postsecondary graduation (4‑year public, 2‑year public, other) and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(12) = 1313.46, Cramer’s V = 0.138, p < .001, N = 22,962【748†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1181.64, Cramer’s V = 0.152, p < .001, N = 17,154【749†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(6) = 498.68, Cramer’s V = 0.160, p < .001, N = 9,691【750†source】

The relationship is moderate but consistent, strengthening slightly by year 10. The main divide is between 4‑year and 2‑year graduates, with different propensities toward statewide vs. regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Almost all graduates remain in postsecondary, but small differences emerge. 2‑year graduates show the highest early regional employment (20.6%), compared to 7.1% among “other” graduates and just 4.5% among 4‑year graduates. Graduates of 4‑year and “other” institutions overwhelmingly remain enrolled (86%+), delaying workforce entry【748†source】.
Year 5: Clearer differences appear. 2‑year graduates lead in regional meaningful employment (40.7%), while 4‑year graduates show higher statewide employment (21.8%). “Other” graduates also lean toward regional work (21.7%). Disconnection rates are somewhat higher among 4‑year graduates, but overall the trend is that 2‑year pathways support stronger early attachment to regional jobs【749†source】.
Year 10: By this point, differences remain. 2‑year graduates sustain the highest regional meaningful employment (45.1%), while 4‑year graduates lean toward statewide meaningful employment (29.5%). “Other” graduates remain in the middle with balanced outcomes. Importantly, no‑record rates are lowest for 2‑year graduates (21.6%), suggesting stronger regional retention. In contrast, 4‑year graduates have higher statewide outcomes but also higher “no record” rates (33.6%)【750†source】.
Overall, institution sector matters: 2‑year graduates show stronger long‑term regional employment, while 4‑year graduates pursue statewide opportunities and are more mobile, and “other” graduates fall between.

Strongest Associations
- The attendance variables (attended within 1st year, ever attended) and postsecondary graduation have the strongest early associations, with Cramer’s V values above 0.5–0.6 at Year 1. These measures clearly separate students who pursue higher education from those who do not, with PS attenders/graduates far less likely to enter immediate regional work but more likely to gain stable employment outcomes over time.
- Highest credential level also shows strong early differentiation, with higher credentials linked to delayed workforce entry and eventual statewide mobility, while lower or mid‑level credentials tie more closely to regional jobs.
Moderate Associations
- PS graduation location and institution sector matter less than attendance or graduation itself but still provide meaningful distinctions. Regional PS graduates are far more likely to remain in local employment, while graduates from 4‑year universities or from outside the region show greater statewide mobility.
Regional Employment Predictors
- Non‑attenders and non‑graduates are consistently more likely to enter regional meaningful employment early, but they also carry much higher risks of disconnection in the long run.
- CTE‑like pathways within postsecondary (2‑year institutions, Associate degrees, regional institutions) show the strongest alignment with long‑term regional workforce attachment.
- Bachelor’s+ degrees, 4‑year universities, and graduation outside MN are consistently tied to statewide employment and mobility, reducing regional anchoring.
Overall Insight
Postsecondary experiences draw a clear line between regional anchoring vs. statewide mobility.
1. Access and completion of postsecondary education lead to broader statewide opportunities and reduced risk of disconnection.
2. Absence of postsecondary pathways results in earlier regional employment but higher long‑term vulnerability.
3. The type, level, and location of postsecondary attainment nuance this divide: regional and 2‑year pathways strengthen local attachment, while higher‑level and out‑of‑region pathways expand opportunities but reduce regional ties.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Highest Credential Level (highest.cred.level)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between highest credential earned and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(20) = 25,119.08, Cramer’s V = 0.366, p < .001, N = 46,777【760†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(20) = 7,371.79, Cramer’s V = 0.231, p < .001, N = 34,683【761†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(12) = 1,030.86, Cramer’s V = 0.132, p < .001, N = 19,828【762†source】

The association is strong in the first year, moderates by year 5, and weakens further by year 10, though it remains significant. The key distinction is that higher credentials (Bachelor’s or above) delay regional employment but lead to stronger statewide employment later, while lower or mid‑level credentials (Associate, less than Associate) are more tied to early and sustained regional employment.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Students with no college are most likely to be in regional meaningful employment (19.9%), but also heavily represented in disconnection categories (44.2% not meaningful, 30.1% no record). Those with some college or Associate degrees show moderate regional employment (18–19%) but are strongly concentrated in “attending PS” (49–69%). Students pursuing a Bachelor’s or higher overwhelmingly remain in education (86.5%) and show the lowest regional employment (5.7%)【760†source】.
Year 5: Regional meaningful employment peaks among less than Associate (42.3%) and Associate degree earners (36.5%), with some college also relatively strong (29.2%). By contrast, Bachelor’s or higher show lower regional attachment (19.1%) but higher statewide meaningful employment (20.5%). Non‑college individuals still show significant disconnection (27.4% not meaningful, 37.0% no record)【761†source】.
Year 10: The regional advantage of Associate and sub‑Associate credentials remains high (42–43%), while Bachelor’s or higher show stronger statewide employment (27.9%) and lower regional employment (26.5%). Non‑college individuals continue to show the weakest outcomes, with the highest disconnection rates (41.7% no record)【762†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that mid‑level credentials (Associate and below) strongly anchor individuals in regional employment, while Bachelor’s and above foster statewide mobility and stronger longer‑term outcomes, and no credential consistently yields the weakest employment stability.

title: Pathways taken after high school - Northeast
text:
Postsecondary Graduation Location (ps.grad.location)
Key Findings
There is a statistically significant relationship between location of postsecondary graduation and post‑graduation outcomes across all timeframes:

1 year after graduation: χ²(9) = 2713.62, Cramer’s V = 0.197, p < .001, N = 23,341【772†source】

5 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 3699.62, Cramer’s V = 0.207, p < .001, N = 28,840【773†source】

10 years after graduation: χ²(9) = 1609.04, Cramer’s V = 0.164, p < .001, N = 19,827【774†source】

The association is moderate in years 1 and 5 and slightly weaker by year 10. The central divide is that regional PS graduates are consistently more likely to work in the region, while graduates outside MN or at MN institutions outside the region are more likely to pursue statewide or out‑of‑state pathways.
Interpretation Over Time
Year 1: Regional graduates show the strongest immediate tie to local jobs, with 65.8% in regional meaningful employment, compared to 23.8% of non‑graduates, 28.7% of MN graduates outside the region, and 22.0% of graduates outside MN. Non‑graduates are most often disconnected (43.4% “not meaningful” and 25.9% “no record”)【772†source】.
Year 5: Regional graduates remain highly concentrated in regional employment (50.2%), far above MN graduates outside the region (18.3%) or graduates outside MN (20.4%). By contrast, MN graduates outside the region have the highest statewide employment (44.0%), reflecting mobility within the state. Non‑graduates remain more disconnected (28.4% “not meaningful” and 31.0% “no record”)【773†source】.
Year 10: Regional graduates sustain a long‑term edge in local employment (43.1%), while MN graduates outside the region remain more mobile (38.0% in statewide employment). Graduates outside MN have lower regional (20.7%) and statewide (17.8%) employment, with a higher share of disconnection (49.4% “no record”). Non‑graduates remain the weakest group, with only 25.6% regional employment and the highest share of disconnection (36.7% “no record”)【774†source】.
Overall, the evidence shows that regional PS graduation strongly anchors individuals in the local workforce, while graduation outside the region or outside MN promotes mobility and statewide attachment. Non‑graduates remain at the greatest risk of disconnection across all timeframes.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
text:
Step 1: Data Preparation and Analytic Population
1.1 Analytic Population
The analytic population is restricted to individuals who: - Graduated from a high school in Northeast Minnesota, - Did not complete a postsecondary credential (ps.grad = No), and

Have complete workforce participation categorizations for years 1 through 5 after high school or,
first 5 years after exiting attendance in a post-secondary institution.

1.2 Annual Workforce Participation Classification
For each individual, annual workforce participation status is identified for: - grad.year.1 - grad.year.2 - grad.year.3 - grad.year.4 - grad.year.5
Each year is classified into one of the following categories: - Meaningful workforce participation - Not meaningful workforce participation - No Minnesota employment record.
1.3 Workforce Disconnection Indicators
For each annual observation, a binary disconnection indicator is created:

Disconnected (year-level) = Not meaningful workforce participation or No Minnesota employment record

Using these annual indicators, individuals are grouped based on persistence of disconnection across years 1–5:

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Disconnected (Broad): Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years

These categories emphasize sustained labor market attachment or detachment rather than point-in-time outcomes.
1.4 Regional Location of Not Meaningful Employment
For years in which individuals are categorized as not meaningfully attached to the workforce, employment location is further classified as: - Within Northeast Minnesota - Outside Northeast Minnesota (elsewhere in Minnesota) - Both (simultaneous employment inside and outside the region)
This classification allows identification of regional underemployment versus regional disengagement.
1.5 Employment Intensity and Job Holding
For each individual and each year (years 1–5), the following employment intensity measures are constructed: - Number of distinct employers during the year - Indicator for multiple job holding (two or more employers)
These measures are used to distinguish underemployment from precarious or fragmented employment.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 2: Descriptive and Summary Statistics
2.1 Distribution of Workforce Disconnection
Summary statistics are produced to describe:

The proportion of non-college graduates in each workforce disconnection category
Differences in persistence and intermittency of disconnection

This establishes the overall scope and severity of workforce disconnection in early adulthood.
2.2 Regional Attachment and Job Structure
Among individuals experiencing workforce disconnection, summary statistics examine:

The location of not meaningful employment (within region, outside region, both)
Average and median number of employers per year
Prevalence of multiple job holding

These summaries clarify whether disconnection reflects local underemployment, out-of-region work, or fragmented employment patterns.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
section: Step 3: Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and Disconnection Trajectories
text:
Step 3: Relationship Between Individual Characteristics and Disconnection Trajectories
3.1 Variables of Interest
The analysis examines associations between workforce disconnection categories and key individual characteristics, including:

Demographics

English language competency
Race and Ethnicity
Income status

High school characteristics

Rural-ness
Average wages
unemployment

High school academics

ACT scores
MCA scores
CTE engagement
PSEO participation

Post-secondary

Attended post-secondary


3.2 Analytic Approach

Categorical variables are examined using cross-tabulations and measures of association (e.g., Cramer’s V).
Continuous variables are examined using ANOVA.
Interpretation emphasizes substantive differences and patterns rather than statistical significance alone.

3.3 Stratified and Comparative Analyses
Where sample sizes permit, additional analyses compare: - Persistently disconnected versus intermittently disconnected individuals - Individuals disconnected within the region versus outside the region - Individuals who transition into meaningful workforce participation versus those who do not
These comparisons help identify which characteristics are associated with stability, recovery, and regional retention.

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Framing and Interpretation
This methodology prioritizes a trajectory-based understanding of workforce participation, recognizing that early-career labor market experiences are dynamic rather than static. By combining persistence measures, regional employment location, and job-holding intensity, the analysis aims to provide actionable insights for workforce development and labor force planning in Northeast Minnesota.

section: Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
text:
Step 2: Identify Workforce State for 5 Years After Formal Education
Next, we need to pull out all the individuals in which we have five years of workforce categories after they either graduate from high school or the last year in which they exited post-secondary attendance.
After that, we will categorize their workforce participation state into the following;

Meaningful WF - NE
Meaningful WF - MN
Not meaningful WF
No MN emp record.

I already created the annual workforce participation states for every individuals one year after graduation through 15 years after graduation. I will bring that list in and filter it by our analytic population.

annual.wf.states <- read_csv("Data/SLEDS/Masters/States/annual-seven-states.csv") %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states) %>%
  mutate(grad.year = fct_relevel(grad.year, "grad.year.0", "grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5", "grad.year.6", "grad.year.7", "grad.year.8", "grad.year.9", "grad.year.10", "grad.year.11", "grad.year.12", "grad.year.13", "grad.year.14", "grad.year.15")) 

no_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "No") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023",
         states != "Attending ps",
         grad.year %in% c("grad.year.1", "grad.year.2", "grad.year.3", "grad.year.4", "grad.year.5")) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  mutate(states = as_factor(states))

last_ps_attendance <- analytic.pop %>%
  filter(attended.ps == "Yes") %>%
  select(PersonID) %>%
  left_join(annual.wf.states, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year)) %>%
  filter(states == "Attending ps") %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  summarize(last_ps_year = max(numeric.grad.year, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() 

ps_attendance <- annual.wf.states %>%
  right_join(last_ps_attendance, by = "PersonID") %>%
  filter(states != "After 2023") %>%
  mutate(numeric.grad.year = str_sub(grad.year, -2, -1),
         numeric.grad.year = str_replace(numeric.grad.year, "\\.", ""),
         numeric.grad.year = as.integer(numeric.grad.year),
         final.year = last_ps_year + 5) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  filter(numeric.grad.year <= final.year,
         numeric.grad.year > last_ps_year) %>%
  mutate(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n == 5) %>%
  select(PersonID, grad.year, states, n)

master.annual.wf.five.year.states <- ps_attendance %>%
  rbind(no_ps_attendance) %>%
  mutate(states = str_replace(states, "Not meaningful, not attending ps", "Not meaningful"),
         states = str_replace(states, "No MN emp record, not attending ps", "No MN emp record"),
         states = ifelse(states %in% c("Meaningful emp County", "Meaningful emp EDR"), "Meaningful emp region", states),
         states = fct_relevel(states, "Meaningful emp region", "Meaningful emp MN", "Not meaningful", "No MN emp record")) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  group_by(PersonID) %>%
  arrange(grad.year) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = seq(n())) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Deeper-Dive Analysis Framework: Non-College Graduates Without Meaningful Workforce Participation
text:
Step 3: Workforce Disconnection Indicators
Next we add another category to determine the level of disconnection, if any, for each individual. Disconnected is defined as any individual that was categorized as not having meaningful workforce participation or no Minnesota employment record in a given year one through five years after exiting formal education.
The level of disconnection is defined as the following;

Persistently Disconnected: Disconnected in 4 or 5 of the first 5 years
Broadly Disconnected: Disconnected in 3 of the first 5 years
Intermittently Disconnected: Disconnected in 1–2 of the first 5 years
Consistently Attached: Disconnected in 0 of the first 5 years


disconnected.level <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  mutate(disconnected = ifelse(states %in% c("Not meaningful", "No MN emp record"), "Disconnected", "Attached"),
         disconnected = as.factor(disconnected)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, disconnected) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  complete(PersonID, disconnected, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  filter(disconnected == "Disconnected") %>%
  mutate(disconnected.cat = ifelse(n == 0, "Consistently attached",
                                   ifelse(n %in% c(1,2), "Intermittently disconnected",
                                          ifelse(n == 3, "Broadly disconnected",
                                                 ifelse(n %in% c(4,5), "Persistently disconnected", "A")))),
         disconnected.cat = fct_relevel(disconnected.cat, "Consistently attached", "Intermittently disconnected", "Broadly disconnected", "Persistently disconnected"))

                          ifelse(quarter == "06", 2,
                                 ifelse(quarter == "09", 3,
                                        ifelse(quarter == "12", 4, 0))))) %>%
  select(PersonID, EmploymentOrganizationID, EmployeeQuarterlyHoursWorked, EmployeeTenure, CountyName, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  mutate(CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, " County", ""),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Saint Louis", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Duluth", "St. Louis"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of Minneapolis", "Hennepin"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "City of St. Paul", "Ramsey"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "Shakopee Mdewakanton Community", "Scott"),
         CountyName = str_replace(CountyName, "White Earth Tribal Counci", "Mahnomen")) %>%
  left_join(counties.regions.1[,c(1,2,10)], by = c("CountyName" = "Name"))

not.meaningful.pop.emp.year <- analytic.pop.annual.wf.states.hs.grad.year %>%
  filter(states == "Not meaningful") %>%
  select(PersonID, emp.year)

not.meaningful.emp.quarter <- not.meaningful.pop.emp.year %>%
  left_join(emp.year, by = c("PersonID", "emp.year")) %>%
  mutate(project.pr = ifelse(is.na(project.pr), "Unclassified", as.character(project.pr)),
         in_region = (project.pr == "Northeast"),
         unclassified_region = (project.pr == "Unclassified"),
         out_region = c(!in_region & !unclassified_region)) %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year, quarter) %>%
  summarise(n.emp = n(),
         any_in_quarter = any(in_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_out_quarter = any(out_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_unclassified_quarter = any(unclassified_region, na.rm = TRUE),
         any_mixed_qtr =  (sum(c(any_in_quarter, any_out_quarter, any_unclassified_quarter), na.rm = TRUE) >= 2)) %>%
  ungroup()

not.meaningful.emp.annual <- not.meaningful.emp.quarter %>%
  group_by(PersonID, emp.year) %>%
  summarize(multiple_emp_same_quarter = any(n.emp > 1),
            max_emp_in_qtr = max(n.emp),
            any_in_region = any(any_in_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_out_region = any(any_out_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_unclassified_region = any(any_unclassified_quarter, na.rm = TRUE),
            any_mixed_region = any(any_mixed_qtr, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(region_location_year = case_when(any_in_region & !any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_only", !any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "out_only", !any_in_region & !any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "unclassified_only", TRUE ~ "mixed" )) %>%
  mutate(
    mixed_type = case_when(
      region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
      any_in_region & any_out_region & !any_unclassified_region ~ "in_out",
      any_in_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_out_region ~ "in_unclassified",
      any_out_region & any_unclassified_region & !any_in_region ~ "out_unclassified",
      any_in_region & any_out_region & any_unclassified_region  ~ "in_out_unclassified"
    ),
    both_structure = case_when(region_location_year != "mixed" ~ NA_character_,
                               any_mixed_region ~ "simultaneous",
                               !any_mixed_region ~ "sequential",
                               TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  select(-any_in_region, -any_out_region, -any_unclassified_region, - any_mixed_region)

Master.annual.wf.states.disconnected <- master.annual.wf.five.year.states %>%
  left_join(Master.not.meaningful, by = c("PersonID", "grad.year")) %>%
  unite("wf.states.refined",
        states, region_location_year, mixed_type, both_structure,
        sep = "_",
        na.rm = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(year.after.exit = paste("after.ed.", year.after.exit, sep = "")) %>%
  select(PersonID, year.after.exit, wf.states.refined) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year.after.exit, values_from = wf.states.refined) %>%
